speechtext:
the second reading of and concurrence in amendments made by the Senate to Bill No. 228, to amend the Income Tax Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, perhaps I should explain that these amendments were made


in the Senate at my request. They refer to the new provision of apportioning interest on securities between interest dates. In the bill as passed by this house it was provided that where a non-resident sold securities to a Canadian, which of course would be sold with accrued interest, the Canadian purchaser would be obliged to deduct 15 per cent nonresident tax from the amount of the accrued interest.
Representations were made to me following the introduction of this measure that this would be liable to cause serious dislocation in the purchase and sale of securities on the international market and that in addition it would cause serious discrimination against Canadian concerns which had offices in the United States-these are small in number-as against those security dealers who have not. The revenue implications of the provision are negligible. As a matter of fact, I think on the sale of securities by residents to nonresidents we will do rather better under the new provision than we did under the old. It seemed to me under the circumstances, since this was a new measure, that it would be well to remove this provision for the deduction by Canadian purchasers of tax on sales by non-residents. For that reason I asked the Senate to make the amendment.

subtopic: APPORTIONMENT OF INTEREST ON SECURITIES- CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: APPORTIONMENT OF INTEREST ON SECURITIES- CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext: It will leave the situation as it was in the sense that we never attempted to collect from a non-resident who sold a bond to a Canadian resident with accrued interest the 15 per cent tax on the portion of the interest which had accrued.

subtopic: APPORTIONMENT OF INTEREST ON SECURITIES- CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not propose to become involved in the complicated nature of the provision that was put in, then changed, and is now taken out. There is one point on which I should like to make a comment. First of all may I point out, in the light of what I have just said, that when the bill came before us it had in section 37 thereof a new paragraph 4A which was to be written into section 97 of the Income Tax Act. When we were in committee of the

whole on the bill on April 10 the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) had his colleague, the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier), move an amendment to strike out 4A as it appeared in the bill that we had before us and to substitute an alternative wording with only a slight difference. We find now that the Senate has deleted that revision of paragraph 4A.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: APPORTIONMENT OF INTEREST ON SECURITIES- CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext: But on my request.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: APPORTIONMENT OF INTEREST ON SECURITIES- CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
I know that the minister says they did it at his request. However, I have pored over this matter to a considerable extent and it seems to me that its effect is as the Minister of Finance has indicated this morning. It does have some effect on the revenues of the country. The minister says that the effect is negligible. I came to the same conclusion, namely, that the effect on the balance of ways and means would not be great and might even improve the position so far as the treasury is concerned. But even if the Minister of Finance requested Their Honours to make the change, I feel that it should not pass without a protest from at least one member of this house. If a rule is a rule, then surely it is supposed to be observed. The other day, when we had another set of amendments to another bill before us from Their Honours, I asked the Minister of Finance if he agreed with me that they did not have the right to amend a taxation measure or, in other words, to make an amendment involving the balance of ways and means. The minister's reply is to be found at page 4516 of Hansard of April 29, 1953. He said:
I wholeheartedly share my hon. friend's views as to the right of private members of the other place to make changes in money bills which affect the balance of ways and means.
I said:
The minister agrees with me that they do not'have that right.
The minister answered:	"Yes." It seems
to me that it does not alter the position for the minister to say the two things that he has said this morning. On the one hand he has said that the effect on the revenue is negligible. On the other hand, he said that the change was made at his request. I should like to know what section of the British North America Act gives the Minister of Finance the right to request the Senate to do something which they are not permitted to do by the terms of the British North America Act. I do not know just how much of a fuss one should create in the circumstances, but it seems to me that the government should have found some constitutional way in which to deal with this question.
Income Tax Act
I have learned a lot about law during the years that I have been in this place, having associated with so many lawyers. Therefore I wonder, if someone should feel aggrieved under this new legislation, whether he might not have the right to appeal to the courts and argue that this change in the Income Tax Act was improperly made because it involved a change in a taxation measure made by Their Honours in the other place. Surely there is a pretty important principle involved here even if the effect on the revenue is only a few cents or a few dollars. Surely a rule is a rule. The British North America Act is quoted to us many times as a sacrosanct document and it provides that money measures, taxation measures, measures affecting the balance of ways and means, are the prerogative of the House of Commons.
As my colleague, the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis), has reminded me, if the Senate can make a change involving a few dollars merely because the amount is small, when the Minister of Finance requests it, then they could make a change that would be quite substantial in nature. Since the Minister of Finance has confirmed the judgment I made on studying this matter, namely, that there is an effect on the revenue, even though negligible, I protest against the way in which this is being done.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: APPORTIONMENT OF INTEREST ON SECURITIES- CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
I have the greatest admiration for my hon. friend's profound knowledge of law acquired during his term of office in the house. The question of the right of the Senate to deal with money bills is of course a very difficult one and very controversial in some respects. The provision of the British North America Act to which he refers is the one which says that any bill which imposes a charge on the people must be introduced in the House of Commons and it must be introduced by a minister of the crown and authorized by resolution.
There are differing opinions as to what the Senate can do to a money bill after it gets there. However, custom and usage over a great many years have determined that they can reject a money bill but that the House of Commons will not accept amendments to money bills made in the Senate except when made on the request of a minister of the crown. That is the practice. So far as I am aware there is no specific provision of the British North America Act which deals with the particular point that we are now discussing.

He said: Perhaps I should give a word of explanation about these amendments.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT LIMITATION ON LENDING    CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext: This is not a money bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT LIMITATION ON LENDING    CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
These amendments were not made at the suggestion of the Minister of Finance, but they are not opposed by the Minister of Finance.
The situation is that section 46 of the bill to incorporate these co-operative credit associations provided that the associations to be incorporated under the act should not invest their funds in loans to any one member in excess of 10 per cent of their paid-up capital and deposits except with the consent


of two-thirds of the full board of directors and except after complying with certain rather strict requirements as to publicity.
In the other place, the question was raised as to whether it was wise to allow this latitude in these new associations. I was asked about it and I said to the banking and commerce committee of the Senate that the provision had been inserted after a good deal of discussion with the promoters of these bills and on the assertion that it would be difficult for them to operate unless a provision of this kind was included in the bill.
The matter was apparently discussed at some length in committee in the other place and, as a result of that discussion, the amendments before the house were proposed. The effect is that the national associations to be incorporated under this bill which is now before the house will be subject to the limitation imposed by section 46-that is to say, they will not be able to lend to any one borrower who is a member of the association an amount in excess of 10 per cent of the paid-up capital and deposits; but that limitation will not apply to the member associations themselves, that is to the provincial organizations which may continue to lend as they do now, I am informed, in excess of those amounts. They will be subject to the limitation that any such loans will have to be approved by two-thirds of the board of directors and publicity will have to be given as indicated in the act. The loans must not be for a period longer than a year and they must be adequately secured.
I am informed that the amendments are entirely satisfactory to the promoters of the bill and since I was prepared to accept the greater-that is to say a similar measure of latitude for the national association it is clear that I can have no objection to the lesser limitation.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GRANT OF CERTAIN TAXES TO CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as you have mentioned, this bill has now come back to the house in committee of the whole from the special committee on radio broadcasting and, as you have said, the bill was reported without amendment. The fact of the matter, Mr. Chairman, is that before the committee one amendment was actually moved and defeated on a polled vote and a further amendment was indicated although not pressed in the committee because the chairman of the committee stated to the committee that he would discuss the content of the proposed amendment with the minister, in order that the matter could be discussed fully in the house, and if the minister saw fit to agree to the amendment it could be proceeded with on that basis in the committee of the whole.
Unless there is some indication of the government's intention to introduce an amendment in the committee of the whole to the effect of the amendments introduced in the committee, then I propose to introduce both amendments in turn. The first one, sir, has to do with the position in which this amendment to the Canadian Broadcasting Act will leave the annual provision for money for the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
Canadian Broadcasting Act I do not propose to repeat what I said in the house on the resolution stage of this measure on April 21, and again on second reading on April 22. I will state the point at issue as briefly as I can and give one or two illustrations of things that are involved in the form of the present section.
The house has already approved an amendment to the Radio Act which has the effect of abolishing the $2.50 licence fee on radio receiving sets. From that source the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in recent years has been receiving a sum of approximately $5f million per annum. The abolition of the radio licence fee was warmly supported in all parts of the house and we, in this Progressive Conservative party, have been asking for its abolition for many years.
There is now the question of providing an alternative or substitute source of revenue for the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. The Minister of Finance in his budget speech indicated that the substitute revenue was to come from the 15 per cent excise tax imposed under the Excise Tax Act on goods within the new section 6 (a) of schedule I of the Excise Tax Act. With the bill before us, reported back from the committee in the same form, we say that what is proposed is something that is going to have continued legislative effect year by year from now until doomsday unless parliament alters the words of the proposed section. It provides, Mr. Chairman, that:
The Minister of Finance shall from time to time grant to the corporation out of the consolidated revenue fund amounts that, in the opinion of the Minister of National Revenue, are equal to the taxes collected under part XI of the Excise Tax Act in respect of the goods mentioned in section six of schedule I to that act.
That is to say, from this time on the Minister of Finance will be authorized to turn over to the corporation without vote of parliament, without mention of it in parliament, without any further authority from or reference whatsoever to parliament, all sums yielded by this excise tax on the goods listed in section 6 of schedule I of the Excise Tax Act. This tax is estimated this year, as was stated to the committee on broadcasting by the deputy minister of finance, to be likely to yield $12 million. The amount is divided almost equally between the goods under sections 6 (a) and 6 (b) of schedule I of the act.
I submit, Mr. Chairman, to this committee that the principle is altogether wrong of parliament saying now, not only for this year but for all future years, that the sums yielded by this particular excise tax shall be paid over to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.

Canadian Broadcasting Act
In the first place, it is my submission that this runs altogether contrary to the principle of parliamentary control over the expenditure of public money. It simply means, if we legislate in this form, that the Minister of Finance is authorized from this time on, whatever this tax may yield, year by year-it may be $12 million this year and in three years' time it may be $20 million or in five years' time it may be $2 million-to hand that money to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. I submit that is a direct contravention of the principle of parliamentary control over public expenditure. There will not be any occasion to refer this matter to parliament. There will be no need of any vote in the estimates. When we are dealing with a principle as important as this, when we are dealing with an institution as important as the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, when we are dealing with matters as important in the life of a nation as sound broadcasting and television, it seems to me to be an urgent matter that parliament should retain complete control over this grant of money year by year.
We defend the principle by insisting upon annual vote by parliament of hundreds of estimates, many of them for smaller amounts than that involved in this section. Why do we do it? We do it because we affirm the principle of parliamentary control, year by year, over the annual expenditure of public moneys. Then, why do we tolerate the complete invasion of that principle in this case? I submit to the committee that the previous section is no adequate precedent for what is provided in the section now before the house. It is true that by section 14 of the broadcasting act, as it stands, there is provision made that the Minister of Finance is to deposit from time to time with the Bank of Canada the proceeds of the moneys collected from the $2.50 licence fee on receiving sets. Now, many of us did not like that provision either, but nevertheless parliament at least had some control over that annual expenditure when parliament was called upon to vote annually an item in the estimates to cover the cost of the collection of the radio licence fee. In recent years this sum increased to approximately three-quarters of a million dollars per annum. However, quite properly, the house has been asked each year to vote that sum of money, and if the majority in this house had chosen not to approve of the $2.50 fee on those radio receiving sets, the house could have ended it by simply refusing to pass the item which made provision for the expenses of collecting the fee.
[Mr. Fleming.!
The matter, therefore, had to come before parliament in the estimates of the Department of Transport every year. Parliament had an opportunity of discussing it, and if a majority had seen fit to disapprove of that method of financing the operations of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, parliament could have refused to pass that item. Under the amendment now before the house, the position is changed in this respect. There is no future amount that will be required to be voted by parliament to make provision for this sum in any respect. It becomes a completely statutory item. There will be no opportunity whatever for parliament even to discuss the matter. There will be no opportunity for parliament to review any question in relation to the adequacy of the amount.
Now, Mr. Chairman, it happens-and this is pure coincidence-that this year the amount estimated as likely to be received from the 15 per cent excise tax on the goods under section 6 (a) of schedule I of the Excise Tax Act is almost identical with the revenue yielded last year to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation by the $2.50 licence fee on receiving sets. It happens to be a matter of pure coincidence, nothing more. I believe the Minister of Finance would be the first to admit it. How do we know what the situation is going to be one year from now? Nobody knows what the situation will be at that time. I do not know of any member in this house who can tell on the one hand, what this tax is likely to yield, and on the other hand what the needs of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation with respect to sound broadcasting will be a year from now. If there ever was a situation where it is imperative that this matter should come back to parliament year by year, surely it is this. Some will recall that a year and a half ago parliament was called upon by the government to vote in advance the sum of $6J million per annum for a period of five years to finance the operations of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. This sum was in addition to the revenue then received by the corporation from the $2.50 licence fee as well as the commercial revenue of the corporation which, of course, continues.
Now, Mr. Chairman, that principle was wrong. The principle of voting annual grants for a period of five years in advance was wrong. If those grants were sound and were needed, parliament should be voting them year by year. The principle of a five-year grant in advance was wrong. Nevertheless,
I say this to those who approved the amendment at that time, this amendment goes even farther:	It proposes that the yield from the

excise tax on these goods I have mentioned should be paid over in perpetuity, not for just five years. That is the effect of this section. It remains a grant, if this becomes a statutory enactment, in perpetuity or until some later parliament amends or repeals it.
In my submission the principle involved here is altogether wrong. Why should there not be a strict maintenance of parliamentary control over the matter so that the money could be granted year by year? In recent days we have had a couple of examples of why it is so important that this house should not let slip through its fingers, in the manner proposed by this section, control over public expenditures in this regard. You will recall, Mr. Chairman, that a question was asked on April 27 by the hon. member for Ontario, as recorded on page 4396 of Hansard for that date, concerning one Zygmund Ziemski, and as, to his employment by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. The third question asked was as follows:
What was the occupation of this man during the two years previous to his employment by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation?
The answer is, "No information". Here is one case where the broadcasting corporation is employing a gentleman on a freelance basis to write important scripts without any previous information as to his employment. In a case of that kind I would think it is obvious that the house would wish information and certainly should have it. Why should the house then put it beyond its powers to insist on information of that kind by passing this legislation in its present form? Then later, Mr. Chairman, on April 30 a question was asked in the house concerning payments made to a particular gentleman for services in connection with broadcasts given by him for the C.B.C.; and as reported at page 4572 of Hansard the Minister of National Revenue said this:
It has not been considered in the interest of the corporation or in the public interest to make public amounts paid by the corporation to individuals in business transactions since the corporation is in competitive positions in engaging services.
I do not accept that as a proper statement of the position which the government ought to take in a matter of this kind; but, Mr. Chairman, if the house is not to be given information on matters of this kind where the answer given by the minister obviously will not hold water, I think it emphasizes why parliament should be so alert to prevent the present control it has over the raising and the expenditure of public moneys from slipping through its fingers in the manner proposed by this section.
Canadian Broadcasting Act
I am therefore moving, seconded by the hon. member for Kamloops:
That section 1 of Bill 340 be amended by inserting in line 7 after the figure (4) the words, "subject to annual vote of parliament".
The effect of that amendment will be that it will be strictly necessary, before those moneys can be paid over year by year, that it should be a matter of vote of parliament. There will have to be an item in the estimates for the purpose. Parliament will have an opportunity of giving or of withholding approval of that item. There will be an opportunity for full discussion not only on the principle of the matter but on the adequacy of the amount proposed. It happens this year that, by a sheer coincidence, the amounts are approximately equal; I refer to the revenue that the corporation lost by the amendment that was passed to repeal the licence fee on radio receiving sets and the amount that is expected to be raised from this new source. But next year the two amounts may not be in balance at all. I therefore submit that this amendment is strictly necessary not only to preserve the principle of parliamentary control but also so that parliament may proceed intelligently next year to meet the needs of the corporation as those needs will be known at that time.
Then I wish to make one final point. There is only one excuse or pretext that has ever been given as to why parliament should be parting in this reckless manner with control over public moneys. It is said to us that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation should have assurance in future years of certain revenues in order that they may go ahead and plan for the future. Mr. Chairman, I am as conscious as is any member of this committee of the need for planning in these matters. I do not wish to see the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation take a short-term view of its responsibilities. But cannot the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation trust parliament to proceed conscientiously year by year and to make intelligent and adequate provision for the needs of the corporation year by year as those needs are known and are disclosed to the house? Why should the shoe be entirely on the other foot?
We are expected, as a sovereign parliament, to trust the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to the extent that in the one case we make provision in their behalf for a five-year annual grant in advance totalling $31| million. Now we are to be asked to turn additional revenue over to them without any future control on the part of parliament over it. Why cannot the alternative and sound principle apply, namely that the

Canadian Broadcasting Act Canadian Broadcasting Corporation trust parliament to make whatever provision is needed year by year in order to meet the known needs of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation? That is an issue, Mr. Chairman, which is presented by this section and which can be overcome only by an amendment of the type that I have proposed.
When this amendment has been disposed of,
I shall have another amendment to the section dealing with the other point raised in the committee concerning the division of the revenue from the excise tax as between sound broadcasting and television. That does not arise under this present amendment. This present amendment is a far-reaching one and the principle involved in this section in its present form is, in my submission, a far-reaching one upon which the committee should take a strong stand.

Mr. Chairman, I was not going to say anything on this bill until the hon. member for Eglinton presented his amendment. I now feel that I should speak to it and state that we in this group are thoroughly in favour of the amendment; and I am going to state our reasons.
When the bill was before the radio committee, the hon. member for Eglinton urged that the committee report the bill with this amendment; but we struck a sort of gentlemen's agreement with the chairman of the committee to the effect that if the bill was reported back "as is", he would talk with the appropriate officials-the Minister of National Revenue and the Minister of Finance-to see whether he could not persuade them to put such an amendment in the bill.
I am reminded by those around me that I am referring now to a second amendment. However, be that as it may, I feel that an amendment of this kind which would place in the hands of parliament the authority over the appropriation is approximate and justified.
I cannot see why the government would not welcome an amendment of this kind. If, however, they oppose it, I think the minister should rise in this chamber and give us most excellent reasons for doing so. If he does not do so, and if the amendment is voted down with no explanation as to why the government opposes it, we can only conclude that such action carries with it a strong implication that the government do not want radio appropriations to be discussed in the House of Commons. If there is any foundation for such a conclusion, then we have to ask, "Why not? Why is it that the government does not want appropriations to be discussed in the house? Have they something


to hide, or would the matter of a discussion be embarrassing to them?" All I can say is that that is exactly why parliament sits here six months or more every year, not particularly to embarrass governments but to protect the taxpayer in seeing that governments do not take from the taxpayer any more than is necessary to carry on the country's business and to see that the taxpayers' money is properly spent.
I would mention this fact. We in this group have not vigorously opposed the general principle of the bill, namely that the radio licence fee should be discontinued and in its place there should be substituted the excise tax on radios, television sets, parts and so forth. And I think it is, if I may use a rather strong term, only decent that the government should indicate that, since that general principle in the bill has not been too vigorously opposed, they should meet parliament at least half-way so that the appropriation would be voted each year by parliament.
I believe the arguments are all in favour of the amendment. I am looking at the matter as fairly as I can. For these reasons we in this group will support the amendment.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GRANT OF CERTAIN TAXES TO CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there are two or three things I have to say about the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Eglinton. First I should like to offer some comment as to the form of the amendment- or perhaps my comment would be as to the form of the subsection as it would be amended thereby.
I do not rise to assert that it is out of order; but it does strike me that it would make a rather ridiculous subsection if it were enacted in the manner proposed by the hon. member for Eglinton. There are two ways of voting money in parliament. One of these is to pass a statute in the proper way, making provision for payments as specified in that statute. The other is to put an item in the estimates which, in due course, becomes part of an appropriation act.
In this instance the hon. member for Eglinton is proposing that we pass a statute which says that money shall be paid from year to year, but only if there is an item in the estimates from year to year. Does that not take on the appearance of a somewhat ridiculous proposal? In my view it should be either one way or the other. Either it should be a statutory provision, or this section should not be written into the law at all.
In other words if the hon. member for Eglinton wishes to achieve the purpose he has in mind it seems to me he should vote against the section of the bill, and argue

that instead of dealing with the matter in this way the government should be asked to put an item in the estimates each year. I need not pursue that aspect of the matter further. As I say, it may be in order for parliament to pass legislation of this kind, but I think it would make us look rather ridiculous if we did it in this way. We do not do it in respect of an ordinary money bill. The Old Age Security Act does not say that we will pay certain money to our old age pensioners subject to an annual vote by parliament. I could go on down the list of the many bills passed by parliament, and make the same comment. Once they are passed they become law-subject always to the right of parliament either to amend those laws or to repeal them. Therefore I have raised this question as to the form of the proposed amendment and, shall I say, as to the means suggested by the hon. member for Eglinton for achieving the purpose he has in mind.
And now, as to the purpose itself, I must say we do not agree with it. It has already been indicated by the stand taken by our members in the special committee on broadcasting that we are opposed to this amendment. We feel-and I might as well be frank about it-that this is just another effort on the part of those who are opposed to public ownership and public control of radio to snipe at the C.B.C.
I am not one who will say that the C.B.C. is perfect; but we still stand by the principle that the airwaves of this country belong to the people of Canada, and that they should be under public control in a manner such as now obtains. We still stand by the principle asserted by the late Lord Bennett in connection with this matter, and we feel that the action now being proposed by the hon. member for Eglinton is an effort to restrict the work of the C.B.C. by making this money available to them only on an annual basis, so that the corporation will not know where it stands from year to year. To me that is just a part of the campaign against the C.B.C.
I think a far more responsible attitude on the part of parliament is to establish a principle, and lay it down in a statute, so that this corporation, acting on behalf of parliament and the people of Canada generally, will know where it stands.
And so, as I have already said, I question the form in which the hon. member for Eglinton attempts to achieve his purpose, and I also indicate our opposition to that purpose. We think parliament should pass the legislation in the form in which it is submitted, without the proposed amendment.
Canadian Broadcasting Act
The hon. member for Macleod raised the question as to whether it was the desire of the government to avoid discussion of radio matters in parliament. It seems to me we have had almost as much discussion about radio as we have had about wheat, and that is a good deal. We have it every year, in one form or another.

The Minister of Finance says the South Saskatchewan dam is a close third. Well, I think it is at the top of the list right now, and it probably will continue to be until the government straightens itself out on that very important issue.
At any rate, I find it difficult to go along with the suggestion that any attempt is being made to restrict discussion of radio and television in this House of Commons. I think it is well that we should have these discussions in parliament from time to time. I regret it does not seem possible for the C.B.C. and C.A.B. to reach an armistice in their difficulties, and to go along for a while on a co-operative basis.
I had the privilege of substituting on the radio committee in the fall session of 1951, and I recall that at that time hope was expressed-certainly by the C.B.C., and I think it was shared by the C.A.B.-that once policy had been agreed upon, these two bodies could work together. But no sooner had that agreement been reached and the understanding arrived at, than immediately attacks began to come in the form of memoranda and briefs against the principle of public ownership of the airwaves of this country which, after all, belong to the people.
And because those airwaves are more limited than, we will say, the space required for the operation of the railways, I suggest that the comparisons usually made do not apply, and that parliament should reaffirm its belief in public control and public ownership in radio, to the extent we now have it, and that we should not impose limitations upon that principle such as would be involved in the amendment now suggested by the hon. member for Eglinton.

parliament should reaffirm the supremacy of parliament. That is the issue, as I see it, before this committee. In order to answer the 'argument regarding the supremacy of parliament, my hon. friend who has just resumed his seat has decided to bring out an argument which after all is not an argument. Because we in this parliament insist and

Canadian Broadcasting Act have been wide awake to the need of the preservation of the parliamentary institution in its entirety he chooses to use the ill-chosen phrase "sniping at the C.B.C." No one in this party has challenged the question as to the need of a national radio. No one is challenging it by this amendment. What we are asking is that parliament shall exercise control over the amount of supply to be voted, and that no institution in this country shall be in the position of receiving a vote in advance, whether that vote is needed or not. Parliament should not 'give u>p its right to ascertain whether the need for money is apparent in each and every year, nor should it -continue to approve a denial- to it of the right to examine expenditure.
I listened to my hon. friend this morning dealing with the power of the Senate. This is a constitutional question, and he spoke forcibly this morning when he said that the Senate had no right to interfere in any way with money bills voted by the House of Commons- anid sent there. He spoke with the same certainty but a few minutes ago. In order to keep the record -clear, and to show that the certainty with which he spoke this morning as- to the power of parliament and the Senate was expressed in words similar to those that he has just used, I would refer to the power of the Senate because the same question may -come up in connection with the matter now before the committee.

Suffice it to say that, if the present bill -goes to the Senate, the Senate as has been held by such an authority as Professor Dawson of Toronto University has the right to make any -change it will in this particular section. Parliament -continues year by year to abdicate too many of its- powers to boards and institutions it has itself set up. This is but another example. The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is in a position where it requires money from time to -time. Surely parliament should not be asked to turn over to the -C.B.C., in advance of the need- of these moneys, -a vote in perpetuity, to use -the apt expression of the hon. member for Eglinton. What parliament is doing by a-n apparently innocuous amendment is to permanently abdicate the power of examination and parliamentary control over moneys it votes.
TMr. Diefenbaker.]

One argument has been answered by my hon. friend, but there is the other argument that these are short -cuts. Someone has said that they save time. Well, parliament does not operate that way. We are not trying to take short cuts through the traditions and fundamental needs and responsibilities of parliament. If we wanted to take a short cut, all we -would need to do would be to elect a cabinet for the Canadian people and then nothing more would need to be done; you would- have your executive -chosen. But that would not be parliament. It is not like parliament to give to a board, however estimable that board may be, and regardless of its needs, the power to receive moneys for years in advance, or at any rate until -another parliament determines to the contrary.
There certainly has been a very pronounced tendency during the present session for the government to close down the lid on all information that might be embarrassing to them. There have been many examples of that, and we in the opposition have taken a strong stand against it. Therefore, we cannot in conscience accept the proposition that we are to turn over to the C.B.C. moneys in advance and be denied a careful examination of the accounts of the C.B.C.
Someone will say that we have a committee. Unfortunately this year I was unable to sit on that committee, as I have through the years. The committee receives a general outline as to what the C.B.C. has done during the year and its plans for the future, but it never has been allowed, neither has the house, to ascertain information of a particular nature. My hon. friend has mentioned a couple of questions that have been brought before the house where there has been a refusal by the government of the information. We have had the same in other departments, such as Central Mortgage -and Housing Corporation. We vote money and they spend it; but try to get any information, just endeavour to ascertain the facts. The situation as it exists in that corporation or in any other government corporation-I am not singling it out- is that the invariable -answer given is that parliament is not entitled to the information.
This latest amendment to the Canadian Broadcasting Act will in effect constitute approval in advance by parliament of the lid being placed on information as to the expenditure of moneys to be made by the C.B.C. for as long as the amendment remains in effect. What we are doing is to give up the right of parliament to be shown the need for supply. What we are doing in effect is turning over to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation a fixed sum of money, whether required or not, for years ahead, without the

need of an annual vote. It may be a shortcut and it may save a few minutes of the time of parliament, but it constitutes a retrograde step and one which I personally would oppose no matter from what side of the house it was introduced.
I reiterate once more the words with which I commenced. I do not think the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre was adding anything to the force of his argument by ascribing to this party motives which he ought to have known were unjustified in order to place himself in the position where he could oppose the amendment suggested by the hon. member for Eglinton.

In my budget speech I indicated that it was proposed to earmark the special excise tax revenues on radio receiving sets and parts and on television sets and that the amount of that tax would be paid over to the C.B.C. I will readily concede that the practice of earmarking taxes for special purposes is one which

Canadian Broadcasting Act should be used with care. We have already created one precedent by, in effect, earmarking three special taxes, the 2 per cent tax on corporations, the 2 per cent tax on personal incomes and the 2 per cent general sales tax for purposes of old age security.
The proposal now before the committee constitutes a statutory appropriation just the same as any other statutory appropriation. Obviously in a tax of this kind some discretion must be given to the Minister of National Revenue because, by reason of the way in which these taxes are collected, it would be impossible for him to determine to the. last cent the exact amount received from these particular taxes. We believe that payment to the C.B.C. of the amount of revenue received from the 15 per cent special excise tax on radio sets and the taxable parts and accessories for them does provide a satisfactory alternative-
An alternative to the radio licence fee.
-at least for the next few years until the present statutory grant for radio broadcasting is reviewed at the end of its five-year term. Consequently we are proposing that the broadcasting act should provide for this transfer of revenue, as well as that for television . . .

It is, of course, exactly the contrary. It is an attempt to ensure that public control of radio shall be preserved, which is the control exercised by parliament. The mere fact that there is a Canadian Broadcasting Corporation with a board of governors consisting of eleven persons does not mean that there is public control of radio broadcasting or television in Canada. In itself, that is no guarantee that broadcasting or television will be carried on in the public interest. The only thing that can ensure the protection of the public interest is for this parliament to maintain its control over the activities of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, because parliament is in a position to insist that the corporation, its chairman and board of governors should account to parliament for what they have done with the money the taxpayers provided.
The mere fact that there exists a board of governors which will no longer have to answer to parliament, if this bill passes in its present form, is no assurance that there shall be public control of radio. Well, Mr. Chairman, I shall try to abide by your ruling and keep to the subject matter of the clauses in the bill, and the amendments thereto.
Apparently the amendment is brought in for the purpose of indicating that under the present bill parliament will not be able to 'exert any control over the financing of the C.B.C. That, I take it, is the basis upon which the amendment is predicated. I think those of us who are familiar with the deliberations of the House of Commons must realize that, even though some of the dire predictions made by members of the Progressive Conservative and Social Credit parties were to come true-particularly in connection with the way in which the C.B.C. will be financed

and even though there were no items in the estimates in the future for the C.B.C., we must remember that the Minister of National Revenue, who is responsible to parliament, will still have to bring his estimates before the committee each year. And as the minister responsible, the minister to whose department the affairs of the C.B.C. are assigned, it seems to me there would be ample opportunity for any member of parliament wishing to debate the subject of C.B.C. financing to do so when that minister's estimates are introduced.
That is one way in which the matter of C.B.C. financing can be debated. Then, again, opportunity is afforded to any hon. member wishing to avail himself of it to move an amendment to a motion going into supply, upon which occasion he may bring forward any grievance he may have regarding C.B.C. financing.
Neither members of the Progressive Conservative party nor of the Social Credit party are very backward in doing this. And while I am just as interested as any member of either of those parties in maintaining the

supremacy of parliament, I fail to see how the bill now before us will undermine that supremacy, so far as the C.B.C. is concerned. As a matter of fact, if I may be permitted to say so, I consider the move now being made by the Progressive Conservative party through the introduction of this amendment, and the support given to it by the Social Credit party, as being simply a way of camouflaging the policy of both those parties in connection with the C.B.C. I do not ask anyone to take my word for this. All he needs to do is to read the pages of Hansard, to look through the debates which have already taken place, and he will find set out very clearly on those pages the fact that the two political parties who are today supporting this amendment, through the years have supported C.A.B. just as intently as if they had been directly sent here to do that. You will find that any recommendations which have been put forward by C.A.B. as opposed to C.B.C. have had the support of the two groups which today are supporting the amendment now before the committee.
I suppose the Progressive Conservatives can hope to draw some comfort from the fact that it was their predecessors, the old Conservative party, that gave Canada the C.B.C. in the first place. But we have come a long way from that. Under pressure from private enterprise and from the Conservatives and Social Crediters the government have retreated a long way from the original position of the Conservative party that introduced C.B.C. to us. It was then vizualized that we should have an out and out publicly-owned radio broadcasting system. We have gone a long way from that.

I am going to read
Canadian Broadcasting Act it. After all, this is an important matter and it is important that the facts should be in everybody's mind. What the hon. member for Vancouver East said was this: I have been here a long time and I have yet to hear one good word, either from those to my right or from those to my left, with regard to the C.B.C.
Having read that, I wish to read briefly from the remarks made by the leader of this party on March 18, as reported on page 3076 of Hansard. After reviewing the situation at some length, the Leader of the Opposition said:
Mr. Speaker, the party which was responsible for the creation of a publicly-owned broadcasting system in Canada, the party which brought the C.B.C. into existence, believes that the C.B.C. should be protected, and should be at all times removed from government interference which will be detrimental to the operation of that system for the gener.al advantage of the people of Canada. Any time we have raised objection to interference with the C.B.C. by this government, we have done so in the belief that the C.B.C. has played, can play and will play a vitally important part in the cultural development of this country. It would be the hope that we will not again hear such a misrepresentation of the facts as we heard in this house yesterday.
And, I regret to say, as we saw here today.
This government is not uninformed in regard to what has taken place. This government knows quite well that in the case of educational broadcasts, which are of such immense value to the people of Canada, those come under the supervision of the provincial departments of education because education is still exclusively the responsibility of the provincial governments. I have had excellent experience in the remarkable work done by the C.B.C. in the field of education. For a while I had some responsibility for the educational broadcasts going out to the schools in one province, and to the children at home. I received the utmost co-operation, the most wholehearted support, in broadcasting the types of programs that the department of education of that province thought would be of advantage to the young people. From conferences I have attended where ministers of education from other provinces were present, I know the same experience has been common throughout Canada. There has been remarkable co-operation between the C.B.C. and the departments of education in broadcasting educational programs in French and in English in every part of this country.
The C.B.C. has given excellent service to this country through the Farm Forum which regularly permits discussion, over the radio of the problems of the farmers, so they may hear the views the farmers exchange concerning this great and basic industry of Canada. Every day the farm news, which digests the latest prices and interesting information concerning farm activity, goes out across Canada and is of great advantage to the farmers. In many cases they arrange their day so' they are in their homes to hear this excellent broadcast. The people right across this country have come to appreciate the news broadcasts which

Canadian Broadcasting Act go out over the C.B.C. I have stated ray own belief that there are no better broadcasts going out over the radio stations of any country of which I know than the regular news broadcasts going out over the C.B.C. Where there has been criticism, it has been in cases where there has been interference with that measure of independence which is so important to the C.B.C., as it is to the private stations as well.
I could read more.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANT OF CERTAIN TAXES TO CORPORATION
speechtext: This has been a most interesting discussion. As the committee knows, I am only pinch-hitting at this time because my colleague, the Minister of National Revenue, through whom the C.B.C. reports, was unable to be here today. I have not cared to intervene because I did not want to interrupt the discussion. speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANT OF CERTAIN TAXES TO CORPORATION
speechtext:
By intervening on several occasions during the discussion I have indicated that it appears quite certain that some parts of the debate that has taken place were not entirely in order. But apparently hon. members, in explaining why this amendment was necessary, have given other hon. members the thought that perhaps the purpose of the amendment was different from that which was acknowledged, and that is the reason why there has been a discussion with respect to the differences of opinion between political parties as to what the C.B.C. should be.

The amendment moved by the hon. member for Eglinton was as follows:
That section 1 of Bill 340 be amended by inserting in line 7 after the figure (4) the words, "subject to annual vote of parliament".
My first reaction was that the amendment was not out of order, that it was merely a change in the wording of the section. The first point I should like to make is to refer hon. members to the citation in Beauchesne where it says that no condition should be attached to a grant. The amendment would attach conditions to a grant, and if it were intended to do so the resolution containing the Governor General's recommendation should have included this wording.
Having listened to the discussion that took place this morning, particularly the remarks made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, the hon. member for Eglinton and the hon. member for Kamloops, I searched the authorities further. It seems to me that the amendment is in opposition to the principle which the bill seeks to affirm. That principle was adopted on second reading. Therefore in the first place, if it was desired to provide for such an amendment, it should have been discussed then.
In the second place, I would ask hon. members to consider this situation. The C.B.C. exists by reason of an act of parliament and some expenditures are authorized. All acts of parliament and the authorities under them are supervised by ministers of the crown. They are responsible for operations and activities carried on under these various acts of parliament. If fixed expenditures have to be recommended, it is done through the Minister of Finance in the course of his budget message and the estimates which are tabled and are analysed in committee of supply. Expenditures on the part of the C.B.C. are authorized by an act of parliament. They have been announced in the budget speech this session, and therefore it remains to be decided whether the expenditures are going to be made by an estimate, the amount of which would be contained in a resolution, or whether it is to be done by statute. Parliament has full authority to take whichever course it wishes. I would like to refer hon. members to citation 518, the last part of which, referring to the House of Commons, reads:
They are entitled to order and dispose how the national revenue, whether permanent or annually granted, is to be spent, and to do so in the greatest detail.
The course that was proposed to be followed and which was adopted in principle on second reading was that this grant be made not by
Canadian Broadcasting Act submitting an estimate to parliament but that it be made by statute on the basis-
-equal to the taxes collected under part XI of the Excise Tax Act in respect of the goods mentioned in section six of schedule I to that act.
To continue, if hon. members will look at citation 476 which indicates the power of the committee of supply they will see that it provides:
The committee of supply controls the public expenditure by considering the grants of money that will be required by the government for the services of the year, upon the estimates of expenditure presented by the ministers of the crown.
The committee of supply shall meet upon a resolution that the house will at a specified time resolve itself into a committee to consider the supply to be granted to His Majesty.
Citation 477 provides:
The estimates for the year are submitted to the committee of supply by the finance minister bringing them down in the house with a message from the Governor General which is read in English and French, the house standing, by the Speaker or by the Clerk at the table. The minister then moves "that the said message, together with the estimates, be referred to the committee of supply."
I have read the citations to indicate that whatever money is to be spent, whether it is authorized by statute or whether it is authorized by the adoption of an estimate in committee of supply, the committee of supply is the agency that controls expenditures-no matter in what form they are agreed to by parliament. Therefore, if hon. members wish to discuss further expenditures made by the C.B.C., even if this amending bill is enacted, they will have the opportunity to do so- because the Minister of National Revenue is responsible for the operation of the C.B.C.- on the first item of his estimates, which is the administration of the Department of National Revenue.
It seems to me that this amendment would destroy the bill. It is against the principle that was agreed upon on second reading and, in the last analysis, a vote against amending clause 1 would allow hon. members to reach the same objective because the amendment is a direct negative.

Your first point is that the house has in effect agreed to the principle of the bill- and the principle of the bill is that this will be a statutory item. With great respect I submit to you that it is not the principle, the essential principle of the bill. The essential principle of the bill is, there being such an identity at the present time between the revenue estimated to be yielded by the tax under the new schedule of the Excise Tax Act and the amount hitherto received by the C.B.C. from the $2.50 licence fee on radio receiving sets,

Canadian Broadcasting Act that, for the future the Minister of Finance should be authorized to pay over such amount as the Minister of National Revenue estimated to be yielded from the revised schedule of the act.
With great respect, Mr. Chairman, that was the principle involved in this bill on second reading. It was not that it should be made a statutory item. The whole tenor of the discussion, right from the time the measure was referred to in the budget speech of the Minister of Finance, and the speech of the Minister of National Revenue at the resolution stage, and his speech on second reading, emphasized the point that this was a matter of a new method of financing which rested for its purpose on the identity of these two sums. That is, in my submission, the only principle the house accepted when giving this bill second reading.
The other answer is that I do not see how an amendment like this could be introduced on second reading. This is not the type of amendment which the rules of the house permit to be introduced on second reading. So much for those points.
With respect to the principle of the bill,
I think the essential' principle of Bill No. 340 is clear from its terms, and it is clear from the tenor of the discussion in various sections of the house that the understanding attached to the principle of the bill is different from that which you have just stated.

In addition to being a
method of financing it might also have been to assure a stability of revenue. The revenues derived from the licences as we knew them had to be supplemented by an additional amount and, to replace that additional amount, we have to vote a sum beyond the money yielded from the collection of tax. Mr. Chairman, I did not make the statement in any invidious sense. I wish to make that clear. What I wished to convey to you is that I think the second ground you put forward is not a question going to the matter of order. We have accepted what we consider to be the principle of the bill- that the C.B.C. must have revenue. That revenue must be made available by parliament, but we say that it should be done in another way.
You point out that there may be opportunity for general discussion on the first item of the estimates of the Minister of National Revenue. That may well be so-a general discursive discussion; but that does not go to the point I was raising this morning. There will be no opportunity for parliament then ever to grant or withhold that money. It is all disposed of.
Moreover, Mr. Chairman, there is no opportunity for parliament to consider the sufficiency of the amount. It happens that this year it appears that there is going to be, according to the estimate made by the deputy minister of finance, an equation. But next year, it may be far from an equation. The submission I was making was that it should be within the power of parliament to consider the sufficiency of the amount, whether it be insufficient, whether it be sufficient or whether it be more than is reasonable. These

questions should all be open to parliament to decide.
Mere discussion on the first item of the estimates of the Minister of National Revenue will not fulfil the need, which is that parliament should have full control over the matter. Therefore the ground upon which you have sought to base your proposed ruling is, I suggest with great respect, not sound as related to the point before us. I am prepared to meet it, when we debate it, as a question going to the merits of my amendment, but on the point of order I say with great respect that it does not relate to the point of order.
On the matter of the first point, if the principle is that the C.B.C. should have revenue,
I quite agree that the house has accepted that principle. The acceptance of that principle, however, does not in any way prevent the introduction of my amendment.

speechtext:
No, Mr. Chairman. I indicated earlier that I have an amendment to introduce on section 1. This is also a matter which I raised in the committee on broadcasting. This matter was not pressed to a vote in the committee because the chairman of the committee suggested that he be given an opportunity to discuss it with the minister. The bill was reported to the house without amendment on that basis. I gather that the chairman of the committee has discussed it with the minister; and from the intimation I had from the minister at one o'clock I gather that he is not prepared to accede to the suggestion embodied in the amendment. I therefore propose to speak about it now, Mr. Chairman, and to introduce another amendment.
This matter goes back to the budget speech of the Minister of Finance in which he outlined an entirely new basis for financing the operations of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. The essence of the new method was, as nearly as possible, to bring about a situation in which those who derived the benefits would bear the expense.
The matter was approached in two parts. There was the new method of providing revenue for the sound broadcasting activities of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to replace the revenue lost to that corporation with the repeal of the $2.50 licence fee

on radio receiving sets, and the minister repeated again this morning the underlying view that he put forward in the budget speech in that respect, namely that radios are now in such general use that the licence fee could be repealed and a tax of general application should replace it.
Then as to the financing of the television activities of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, it was proposed by the minister that a similar provision be made to permit the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to have as a source of revenue the sums yielded to the public treasury from the excise tax on television sets and tubes. I think I must read a passage from the budget speech of the Minister of Finance because it may be that he is not going to share the interpretation which I have put upon it and which I think is the only interpretation it can properly bear. That interpretation is that two funds were to be created, that they were coming from separate sources and they were going to separate uses, and that they were not to be merged in one general fund. This is what the minister said as reported at page 2133 of Hansard of February 19:
There is one further subject on which I have important changes to announce. The government has been seeking a fair and effective source of revenue for the national system of television broadcasting being developed by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in accordance with the general policy that was announced by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent). The government's policy is to have the cost of the national television service paid, as far as that is practicable, by those who benefit from such service. It also wishes the C.B.C. to have a direct source of revenue, on which it can budget over a period, and not to be dependent upon annual appropriations to finance its operations. We wish to emphasize that it is a separate corporate body, under the general control of parliament but not a part of the government.
Television operations have just recently commenced and their development has been financed by loans specifically authorized in the estimates. It is now expected that, in addition to commercial television revenues, the C.B.C will require about $6 million in the next fiscal year to meet operating costs of television, including interest on loans. This requirement will increase over the next few years, perhaps to about $10 million. Some part of these needs during the development period may properly be met from loans* and paid from future revenues, but we should start now with a plan to provide adequate revenues over the long run.
It is therefore proposed that the Canadian Broadcasting Act should be amended to provide that the corporation should in future receive from month to month the amount of revenue yielded by the present 15 per cent special excise tax on television sets and the picture tubes for such sets, and on such parts and accessories for television sets as are taxable under the Excise Act. In this way those who buy sets, or the replacement tubes for them, will be providing the basic revenue necessary for C.B.C. television services. In order to make this plan effective, it will be necessary to : revise the regulations to provide that tourists returning to Canada may not include as baggage eligible
Canadian Broadcasting Act
for free entry television sets or the picture tubes for use in them.
Having decided upon this plan in regard to television, we have now come to the conclusion that a similar transfer of the 15 per cent special excise tax revenue can and should be made to assist in financing radio broadcasting in place of the present licence fee. Although the continuation of this fee had been recommended by the Massey commission, experience has convinced us that it is uneconomical to collect such a small individual fee from such a high proportion of Canadian families, if any satisfactory alternative is open. We believe that payment to the C.B.C. of the amount of revenue received from the 15 per cent special excise tax on radio sets and the taxable parts and accessories for them does provide a satisfactory alternative, at least for the next few years until the present statutory grant for radio broadcasting is reviewed at the end of its five-year term. Consequently we are proposing that the broadcasting act should provide for this transfer of revenue as well as that for television, and that the order in council under the Radio Act setting the present licence fees of $2.50 should be revoked with effect from April 1.
Then further down the page:
I estimate that the amount of revenue to be received by the C.B.C. under these arrangements will be approximately $12 million in the next fiscal year, the amount in respect of radio probably exceeding somewhat that for television. The public will be relieved of paying something over $6 million in radio licence fees, this next fiscal year, and our expenditure in collecting such fees, anticipated at $700,000 in the estimates, will be saved.
Mr. Chairman, I think it is perfectly clear that under the scheme proposed by the Minister of Finance in that speech, and which was approved by the house when it passed the minister's motion that the house should resolve itself into committee of ways and means and when his resolutions were duly reported, what the house approved was a proposal under which the Excise Tax Act should be amended so that radio sets, tubes and accessories should be separated from those relating to television and that the 15 per cent excise tax yielded from that source should then be paid over to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation for radio broadcasting; and similarly that as to the remainder of the goods covered by section 6 and which now are to be found enumerated in section 6(b) of schedule I of the Excise Tax Act, namely television sets, tubes and accessories, the excise tax on those should be made available to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation for the development of television.
The minister was at pains to point out that the revenue from the first source, section 6(a) of the schedule, would just about provide the C.B.C. with the revenue it lost with the abolition of the $2.50 licence fee; and on the other hand that $6 million was estimated to be yielded from the excise tax on television sets and that that would be available to the C.B.C. for television broadcasting and the development of it. Mr. Chairman, the tenor

Canadian Broadcasting Act of the remarks made in this chamber by the Minister of National Revenue on the resolution stage of the present measure, on April 21, as reported at page 4185 of Hansard and again in his speech on the motion for second reading on April 22 as reported at page 4215, is to precisely the same effect. The whole stress was on the fact: You have two funds here, and they are going to two separate objects.
Then when we came to examine this bill in committee we found that the bill did not carry out that division. Bear in mind, will you, that in furtherance of the proposal of the Minister of Finance, embodied in language which I have read, the house did proceed to amend the Excise Tax Act. It amended section 6 in order to create two classes of goods under section 6 thereafter-section 6(a) which now includes radio receiving sets, tubes and accessories, and section 6(b) which enumerates television sets, tubes and accessories.
Now, we have created the distinction very clearly in the statute in the matter of the sources of revenue. We have two sources now. But when we come to this measure, by which provision is to be made for the disposal of the two sources of revenue, for two distinct purposes, we find the bill does not have that effect at all; but that although parliament has indicated two sources this bill sets out one, and one alone, without a word earmarking it by allocation at all to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
When I raised this point in committee some of the members said, "Well, will not the C.B.C. know that this is what is intended?" The answer clearly is that the C.B.C. does not know. The C.B.C., without statutory direction with respect to the $12 million, will not know how parliament intended that the money should be divided as between the two principal activities of the C.B.C., namely radio broadcasting and television. And surely it is the minimum duty of parliament, in dealing with a large sum like this, to be fair to the board of governors of the C.B.C., and say to them how as between these two principal activities of the C.B.C. that money is to be used.
It is impossible to deduce from the fact that parliament has divided into two the sources of revenue, by the amendment made in the Excise Tax Act, that parliament therefore expects the C.B.C. to carry that line of distinction through. The distinction will be preserved in this measure as to the source: but it stops there. The deputy minister of finance, before the committee, said, "We will pass the information on as to how much of the monthly payments comes from the excise

tax on goods under 6(a), and how much from goods under 6(b) of schedule I to the act".
But again, that is no protection to the board of governors of the C.B.C. as to how they are to use this money for these two purposes. It is perfectly clear that the house has already approved, on the authority that you used a few moments ago in dealing with the point of order on the previous amendment-the house has given approval to both parts of the scheme as proposed by the Minister of Finance in his budget speech in the passage I read from page 2133 of Hansard. The house has approved not only that there be two sources of revenue but, secondly, that there be two separate uses made of that revenue.
Unquestionably, this bill does not do that; and it should. The Auditor General in his report-and it will be recalled that this was discussed at an earlier stage-did criticize the C.B.C. in its financial statement for not keeping strictly separate financial accounting of radio broadcasting on the one hand and television on the other; and to the extent to which there had not been a clear separation of the financing of the C.B.C. in respect of those two activities up to that point, he was critical. Now, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, as the chairman made clear to us in committee, has separated those two functions, and it has financial reports with respect to those two functions. Therefore parliament ought to be consistent in the matter of assisting the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in this regard by earmarking those two funds.
This morning the Minister of Finance used the expression "earmarking". That is what he proposed in his budget speech ought to be done now-and only parliament can do it. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Kamloops, the following amendment:
That section 1 of Bill 340 be amended by adding in line 12 thereof after the word "Act" the following words:-
"and that the equivalent of the taxes so collected in respect of the goods mentioned in section six (a) of the said schedule be available to be used by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in relation to sound broadcasting, and that the equivalent of the taxes collected in respect of goods mentioned in section six (b) of the said schedule be available to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to be used in relation to television."
In a word that is simply carrying forward the scheme proposed by the minister in his budget speech, and that was echoed by the Minister of National Revenue in speaking on this measure at the resolution stage, and on second reading. It does something that parliament has done hitherto; because I think it is correct to say that without exception parliament has, in times past, in making funds

available to the C.B.C. either by way of grants, statutory items or loans, always earmarked such items for one purpose or the other-either sound broadcasting or television. Up to the present time provision for television has always been by way of loans, but they have always been earmarked for that purpose. If this amendment is not carried, then it means that we have departed from the principle which has always been followed hitherto by parliament with respect to grants made available to the C.B.C., whether made available by way of grants, statutory items or loans.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANT OF CERTAIN TAXES TO CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, first I should like to put my hon. friend right in the references he has made to my budget speech. I know the quotations he made were strictly accurate; but the statements were in the broadest general terms, and there was certainly no intention in my mind, when I made them, that there should be two separate funds in the C.B.C. accounting, from the two attributed taxes. He said that that was approved by parliament.
Well, he is completely wrong in that. In the course of his budget speech a minister of finance takes occasion to review the general financial position of the country, and to make such announcements as require immediate legislative action.
In the case of the new method of financing the C.B.C., it seemed to me that the budget speech was the proper time to give this information. But the place for the detail of the legislation implementing that action is when the legislation is brought in.
Then, in the second place, when the bill to amend the Excise Tax Act was before the house it was made clear that under sections 6(a) and 6(b) of schedule I, to which my hon. friend referred, the separation was primarily for statistical purposes. As I indicated this morning in my statement, in the case of attributed taxes of this kind it would be impossible for the Department of National Revenue to attribute to the exact cent the amount received from a tax on a particular commodity coming under that schedule. And that is why the section now before us provides the language-
-amounts that, in the opinion oi the Minister of National Revenue, are equal to the taxes collected under part XI of the Excise Tax Act.
Now, on the amendment itself, let me say that I did not have the advantage of serving on the committee. As the house knows, I am acting today on behalf of the Minister of National Revenue; but my information is that this matter was discussed in committee-my hon. friend has indicated that-and that the
Canadian Broadcasting Act majority view in the committee, at any rate, was that it would be unduly restrictive to the C.B.C. to attempt to apportion these two revenues, and to restrict their expenditure of the amounts received to the amount attributed to radio operation on the one hand or to television operation on the other.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANT OF CERTAIN TAXES TO CORPORATION

I accept completely my hon. friend's statement. I was not a member of the committee and this information came to me from my deputy minister. My own personal position is that it would be unduly restrictive on the operations of the C.B.C. to attempt to apportion these two sources of revenue. I made it quite clear in my budget speech that in lieu of the $2.50 licence fee it was proposed to transfer to the C.B.C. the revenue from the tax on television and radio sets. I mentioned that our estimates were that in the coming year the revenue from the tax on television sets and parts would be approximately $6 million and that from radio and the like would perhaps be in excess of that. There was never any thought in my mind that the two items should be separated, and my present view is that they should not be. For that reason I would feel that I would have to oppose my hon. friend's amendment.
Before I sit down I may say that I have been informed that there are a great many young Rotarians sitting in the ladies' and public galleries and I want to extend our welcome to them. I am sure they are being suitably enlightened on the conduct of public business.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANT OF CERTAIN TAXES TO CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I shall not detain the committee except to express our view in respect to this particular amendment. We are inclined to oppose it. We rather agree with the Minister of Finance that it would be a little restrictive. We think that more elbow room would be given in the operations of the

Canadian Broadcasting Act C.B.C. if there was just the one fund to which these revenues went and leave it to the C.B.C. to be fairly free in administering both sound broadcasting and television as they think is in the best interests of the listening public at large.
We do point out that this does not mean that separate accounts will not be kept. We will know how much is collected from the excise taxes on sound radio receiving sets and equipment and how much is collected on television sets and equipment. We will know too how much is spent on sound broadcasting and how much is spent on television. If there is a little overlapping I think we should permit the C.B.C. to do that if they think it is in the interests of radio and television that it should be done.
I think this is one time when we must express confidence that the C.B.C. will be desirous of giving Canadian listeners and viewers the best possible radio and television service they are able to give. I do not think that by allowing them to do so we are depreciating to any extent the value of one department of their activities in favour of another. We have sufficient confidence that they will look after both radio broadcasting and television equally.
I am not vigorously opposed to the amendment but we do feel that we should give enough latitude to the C.B.C. to carry out its own policy with respect to this.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANT OF CERTAIN TAXES TO CORPORATION
speechtext: In our view the difficulties that would arise from this amendment greatly outweigh any advantages that might come from it. In fact I do not really see what the advantages are.
