Mr. Chairman, I think I should state briefly why I feel that the amendment is proper. I suggest to the minister and to the committee that it is not a question of having any lack of confidence in the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to administer these funds and to look after the interests of television and radio broadcasting in Canada. There is no question of lack of confidence in their ability to do that. It is rather a matter of being fair to them by giving them a definite rule or directions as to how the funds should be applied. I do not think it is quite fair to put this body in the position of having to decide what division it will make of the funds which parliament is now authorizing and whether they themselves will take perhaps an extra amount from the revenue derived from the tax on radio parts and use it in their television activities. I think it would be much more acceptable to this 
governing body to have a firm direction as to how they should apply these moneys.
I have not been able to find the transcript as yet, but it is my recollection-I say this subject to correction and I understand the transcript is not out yet-that the chairman of the board of governors did say in reply to a question by me that he expected to receive these funds as it were in two clearly divided amounts and that he expected also to apply them with respect to the fields from which they were initially derived. Of course he is not in a position to state policy in that regard, but that was the impression as to the policy which would be laid down for them to operate under.
That is all that this amendment is suggesting, that parliament should write into the bill a directive to the board of governors of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation so that they themselves will not be under any uncertainty as to how they are expected to apply these funds.

speechtext:
There is one point I should like to raise on section 2. This is the interpretation section and we find the following definition in subsection (c):
"Convention waters" means the territorial waters and the high seas off the western coasts of Canada and the United States and the southern and western coasts of Alaska.
Then in other sections, notably section 5, there is a reference to what are described as "the territorial waters of Canada". That section, as I understand it, gives the Canadian protection officers the right to seize a ship, whether it is Canadian or American, in Canadian territorial waters, and there is the further right for that ship to be subjected to the process of law in Canadian courts. But there is no such right where a United States ship is seized in waters which are not Canadian territorial waters.
This is the third bill this session in which the question of territorial waters has come up. For example, we had Bill No. 293, the North Pacific Fisheries Convention Act, which of course referred to the treaty between Canada, the United States and Japan. In it there was a definition of "convention area" which was as follows:
"Convention area" means all waters, other than territorial waters, of the North Pacific ocean including the adjacent seas.
Again the words "territorial waters" were used in their general application. The third bill was Bill No. 44, the Coastal Fisheries Protection Act. There we find an actual definition of Canadian territorial waters reading as follows:
"Canadian territorial waters" means any waters designated by any act of the Parliament of Canada or by the governor in council as the territorial waters of Canada, or any waters not so designated being within three marine miles of any of the coasts, bays, creeks, or harbours of Canada, and includes the inland waters of Canada.
Halibut Fishery Convention
Therefore it is quite obvious that Canadian territorial waters will be only those waters within three miles of our coast except where other waters have been designated either by act of parliament or by the governor in council.
The question of territorial waters has become of great importance on the west coast. I am sure the Minister of Fisheries will agree with that statement. There are different waters about which a question has arisen as to whether or not they are Canadian territorial waters, but I use as an example Hecate strait lying between the Queen Charlotte islands and the mainland of British Columbia. Under the terms of the Northern Pacific Halibut Fishery Convention Act it will not be possible for a Canadian court to try a United States vessel fishing in the Hecate strait for halibut contrary to the terms of the convention because that strait has never been declared to be Canadian territorial waters.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
subtopic: CONVENTION FOR PRESERVATION OF HALIBUT FISHERY OF NORTH PACIFIC OCEAN AND BERING SEA
speechtext: It is by order in council.

subtopic: CONVENTION FOR PRESERVATION OF HALIBUT FISHERY OF NORTH PACIFIC OCEAN AND BERING SEA
speechtext:
Therefore it would be considered as high seas. Not only does the question arise under the halibut convention act but we also have a situation in the Hecate strait at the moment with respect to fishing for crabs. I asked the Department of Fisheries a question some weeks ago as to the amount of crabs that have been caught by Canadian vessels, United States vessels and vessels of other nations in the Hecate strait during the last five years. The answer will be found at page 3053 of Hansard. Figures were given for the catch by Canadian fishermen, but I was told that no information was available regarding the catch of crabs by United States fishermen, and that it was believed that no vessels of any other nation had been fishing for crabs in the Hecate strait.
A few days ago, on April 28, the parliamentary assistant advised the house that he had obtained information from the United States authorities with respect to the catch of crabs in the Hecate strait by the Americans. I find now from the two reports that the Americans did no fishing for crabs in the Hecate strait in 1948 or 1949 but that they did in the years 1950, 1951 and 1952, and caught a larger quantity of crabs than the Canadians. The figures are as follows: 1950, Canadians, 723,400 pounds and Americans, 880,292 pounds; 1951, Canadians, 838,100 pounds and Americans, 960,749 pounds; 1952, Canadians, 1,105,100 pounds and Americans, 1,169,062 pounds.
I am told by people interested-I cannot vouch for the accuracy of the report-that the Americans have depleted their own crab fishing waters and have moved into the Hecate

Halibut Fishery Convention strait, which in my opinion should be considered to be Canadian territorial waters.
There is also the threat that the Japanese may come there to fish for crabs. According to a press dispatch of March 28 a Japanese crab fishing fleet of 13 ships was to leave in a few days on the first post-war Japanese fishing expedition to Bristol bay, Alaska. If Hecate strait is considered high seas and not Canadian territorial waters they are free to go into Hecate strait and fish for crabs because, as the minister knows, crabs are not covered by the treaty between Canada, the United States and Japan.
The whole question is of concern on the west coast, and I should like to point out again that steps should be taken by Canada to declare Hecate strait to be Canadian territorial waters. That would enable us to deal with the crab situation, and it would also enable us to deal with United States ships fishing in that strait for halibut under this convention which is to be enforced, so far as Canada is concerned, under the provisions of the bill we are now considering.
I place these suggestions before the minister, and I hope he will be able to give the committee some assurance that the situation will be met.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
subtopic: CONVENTION FOR PRESERVATION OF HALIBUT FISHERY OF NORTH PACIFIC OCEAN AND BERING SEA
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as far as the first point is concerned, convention waters in this bill, unlike the other bill-the North Pacific convention-include both the high seas and the territorial waters of British Columbia, the west coast of the United States and the Alaskan shores, with the powers of arrest in those areas. This convention has used this description of convention waters for the last 30 years.
The halibut fishery of the entire waters, both our own waters and the high seas, is under the control of this international commission. If either a Canadian or American ship is found violating the regulations in our own territorial waters, that ship is arrested by Canadian officers and brought before Canadian courts. Similarly, if a Canadian ship were found in territorial waters off Alaska or off the mainland of the United States, which areas are also covered by this convention, then that ship would be arrested by a United States patrol vessel and brought to justice in United States courts under the terms of the American act corresponding to this act. If a Canadian patrol vessel arrests a Canadian ship upon the high seas, it is brought before Canadian courts. If it arrests an American ship that ship is turned over to the American authorities and prosecution is launched by the American authorities. American patrol ships act in similar fashion.


In the three fishery acts mentioned by the member for Vancouver-Quadra there is no definition of territorial waters. Territorial waters are defined in other acts. As the hon. member mentions the delineation of territorial waters is a very difficult question. The matter was discussed at length in the committee. It is always very easy to suggest that a country with rich fisheries off its shores should announce arbitrarily that it will extend its territorial waters from 3 miles to 12 miles, or even to 100 miles as has sometimes been suggested. However, other nations will then claim that they have historic rights in those fisheries acquired over the years. They rely on the fact that the British navy many years ago established the doctrine of the freedom of the seas.
In nations such as ours, with rich fisheries off our coasts, there is always pressure to extend our territorial waters unilaterally- arbitrarily and by unilateral action on our part. Such action was taken three years ago by one European country, which resulted in reprisals being taken by the country excluded, Britain. Those reprisals were not taken by the government of Great Britain but by the ports and labour unions of Great Britain and as was explained in the fisheries committee, repercussions from this action have been responsible for some of the troubles of our Canadian fishermen finding markets in the United States today. It shows the possible ramifications. I am quite sure that if this country were to take arbitrary action today to extend our territorial waters to exclude United States fishing vessels there would be great demands for immediate action in reprisal by the United States fishermen. When you remember that almost 80 per cent of our exported fish is sold to the United States you will see that such action taken unilaterally by us would be very short range, and lead to grave problems.
We are quite conscious of the problem. Some three years ago the United Nations general assembly raised the question for member nations. Each nation has set up a legal committee to study the question so far as their own waters are concerned. Our committee is headed by Dean George Curtis, the dean of law of the University of British Columbia, and it has not yet brought down its recommendations. When it has brought them down we shall proceed in concert with other nations to try to get multilateral agreements on territorial waters which will be respected and which will not lead to the reprisals that would likely result if we were to go ahead by ourselves.
As far as Hecate strait is concerned, it was pointed out to the fisheries committee that by order in council in 1909 Canada did assert

that Hecate strait was territorial water, with this important factor; that the United States had claimed historical use of those fishing grounds. They were the only nation to have used the grounds other than ourselves, and the situation was left as it was. If ships of other nations were to fish in Hecate strait I would expect this government to take appropriate action. The United States however claims to have historic rights, because they have been fishing that area for many years. No decision has ever been pronounced on this assertion.
As far as halibut is concerned it does not matter whether Hecate strait is territorial water or is not territorial water. In either case it would come under the regulations of this convention and United States ships would be as free to fish it as Canadian ships are.

subtopic: CONVENTION FOR PRESERVATION OF HALIBUT FISHERY OF NORTH PACIFIC OCEAN AND BERING SEA
speechtext: There would be a difference in the courts in which offenders would be tried.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
subtopic: CONVENTION FOR PRESERVATION OF HALIBUT FISHERY OF NORTH PACIFIC OCEAN AND BERING SEA
speechtext:
The only difference would be the court in which the offending ships would be tried. I would like to make the comment, however, that in 30 years of this treaty there has never been a suggestion from fishermen on either side of the boundary that the courts of either country have given preferential treatment to their own nationals. Nothing could work out better than that. As far as the halibut fishery is concerned I repeat that whether Hecate strait is territorial waters or high seas this convention would apply and the fishery would be controlled just as it is now for the entire area.
Crab fishing does not properly come under this bill, but it is a matter of interest. There are great quantities of a certain species of crab in Hecate strait and in the waters surrounding the Queen Charlotte islands. We have never been able to exploit them fully because we have never found big enough markets for them. With all due deference to the maritimes this crab is just as succulent and tasty as the eastern lobster but it requires much more labour to prepare for canning or freezing and the crab must be alive right to the point of processing. Labour costs in the crab canneries on the west coast have been so high that there has been only limited market for the products. The fresh market on the west coast is pretty well limited to the areas to which those crabs can be transported alive.
The Japanese have fished in the past off the Alaskan coast in Bristol bay and Bering sea for very large king-size crabs from which they are able to obtain larger pieces of flesh with a consequent lowering of canning costs. The Americans have been fishing crab in
Halibut Fishery Convention Hecate strait, and we have this spring given licences to three Canadian boats to engage in the same fishing and sell their catch in Seattle.
The west coast market for fresh crab has been pretty thoroughly saturated as far as Canadian outlets are concerned. If our fishermen are going to fish them more extensively we will have to look for American markets and, in those markets, they will have to be delivered alive. It means that there is a very limited field for fishing. Crab and ground fish of the west coast are two fish which we, under the terms of the convention to which the hon. member has referred, the international North Pacific convention, should now begin to study scientifically and to conserve with the aim of bringing them under the convention.
That is the position as far as territorial waters are concerned. No matter how our territorial waters are defined, this treaty will apply to them, the only real distinction being made in the powers of arrest of ships within and without territorial waters.

subtopic: CONVENTION FOR PRESERVATION OF HALIBUT FISHERY OF NORTH PACIFIC OCEAN AND BERING SEA
speechtext: Have the Americans any historic right to fish in Hecate strait for crab?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
subtopic: CONVENTION FOR PRESERVATION OF HALIBUT FISHERY OF NORTH PACIFIC OCEAN AND BERING SEA
speechtext: Historic right of fishing has never been tied down to one species of fish. Halibut and cod have been the main fish caught in Hecate strait by Americans in the years since the United States bought Alaska from the Russians. Actually commercial fishing for crab is a fairly recent development for both the United States and ourselves.

subtopic: CONVENTION FOR PRESERVATION OF HALIBUT FISHERY OF NORTH PACIFIC OCEAN AND BERING SEA

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries

subtopic: CONVENTION FOR PRESERVATION OF HALIBUT FISHERY OF NORTH PACIFIC OCEAN AND BERING SEA
speechtext: Can you have a position of that kind, where waters are considered to be Canadian territorial waters except as against the United States?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries

I am no legal authority, and all I can say is that we have a similar situation in Newfoundland along what is called the

Trade Marks Act
French shore. The Newfoundland members can correct my history on this. International law on territorial waters is one of the more obscure branches of law, and that was one of the reasons the United Nations committee was anxious to have it clarified. I am sure the report brought down by Dean Curtis and his advisers will help to clarify the Canadian position.

subtopic: CONVENTION FOR PRESERVATION OF HALIBUT FISHERY OF NORTH PACIFIC OCEAN AND BERING SEA
speechtext: In view of this halibut convention, which has worked so well for many years, is the United States taking a strong stand against Canada declaring Hecate strait as Canadian territorial waters, even as against the United States?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
subtopic: CONVENTION FOR PRESERVATION OF HALIBUT FISHERY OF NORTH PACIFIC OCEAN AND BERING SEA
speechtext: I could not answer that.

subtopic: CONVENTION FOR PRESERVATION OF HALIBUT FISHERY OF NORTH PACIFIC OCEAN AND BERING SEA
speechtext: Is the government planning to take steps in an endeavour to get this situation cleared up so these straits may be declared Canadian territorial waters?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
subtopic: CONVENTION FOR PRESERVATION OF HALIBUT FISHERY OF NORTH PACIFIC OCEAN AND BERING SEA
speechtext: All I can say again is that this order in council, which was mentioned in the fisheries committee, did assert our sovereignty over those waters as long ago as 1909. speakeroldname: Hon. Milion F. Gregg (Minisler of Labour) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: PAYMENT TO INSURED PERSONS BECOMING
speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1940, to provide for the payment of unemployment insurance benefit to insured persons who, while otherwise unemployed and entitled to benefit, become incapacitated for work by reason of illness or injury.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Beaudoin in the chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: PAYMENT TO INSURED PERSONS BECOMING
speechtext:
The effect of the bill to be founded on this resolution will be that a person who is in receipt of unemployment insurance benefit will continue to receive such benefit, notwithstanding the fact that he may be incapable of or unavailable for employment by reason of illness, injury or quarantine.
The law as it now stands requires the unemployment insurance commission to deny benefit to a claimant in respect of any day on which he is incapable of or unavailable for work. These are normal conditions for the orthodox type of unemployment insurance, and they were essential during the early development of the Canadian scheme. We now seek to modify those conditions.
Experience has shown that considerable hardship resulted from the application of the conditions to which I have referred, in that benefits were denied unemployed persons simply because they fell El or were injured. I think that we can all agree that a person who is unemployed, and drawing benefits, needs these benefits when he is sick just as much as and more than when he is well. The desire to do something about it has been in our minds for quite a while, and the delay in putting such a plan into effect has been caused by long and intensive study to see how jurisdictional and administrative difficulties might be overcame. In fact, Mr. Chairman, the extension of this study is the only reason I am so late in the session in introducing this legislation. I believe that most of these difficulties have now been solved in so far as they are related to the step now proposed.
I feel that I should point out to hon. members that this proposal does not extend to the insured worker who becomes unemployed because of sickness or accident. However, benefit can be paid to such a worker after he has recovered from the illness, if no suitable work is then available for him.
There will be no change in the rate of benefit nor in the method- by which the dura-
Unemployment Insurance Act tion of benefit is established. I am unable to give a precise estimate of the added cost to the fund. It is not felt that the plan will add materially to the number of insured persons filing claims for benefit. It will of course increase the number of days for which benefits are paid. It is felt that the proposal can be taken care of, for the present at any rate, without asking for additional contributions to the unemployment insurance fund. I do not believe that the additional cost of administration will be great.
It is realized that the proposed amendment does not go as far as has been suggested by the labour congresses, by some members of this chamber and iby others. However, the plan will give the commission some very useful experience in this further extension of unemployment insurance benefits.
The proposed amendment has been considered by the unemployment insurance advisory committee and that committee has been pleased to report favourably thereon.
I recommend the resolution to the committee.

subtopic: PAYMENT TO INSURED PERSONS BECOMING
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to compliment the minister on this improvement to the Unemployment Insurance Act. I think it is a measure that is overdue. The minister has given some explanation of the reasons why it was not brought in previously. I have felt for a long time that such provision should be made in the regulations governing the Unemployment Insurance Act, because of the fact that, under the old system, undoubtedly discrimination was practised against those people who, by reason of the fact that they registered in large urban centres, were required to report regularly for work to their respective offices whereas in some parts of Canada, where they were in remote areas, they could do so by other means.
Of course, under those circumstances, it was not possible to check up on the health of the applicant. Accordingly if he had the misfortune to become ill or to suffer accident, unless there was work available for him such matters went by the board; no one knew anything -about them at all. Because of this situation, those workers in urban centres suffered by reason of discrimination. Immediately they became ill, the local office knew about it and their benefits ceased.
I do not think this measure is contingent upon the condition of the fund because, as the minister has intimated, I do not believe that the amounts so expended will be large. Hence the condition of the fund will not be jeopardized to any degree at all. I think that a measure such as this one should be predicated upon simple justice, should be a matter

Unemployment Insurance Act of policy, and should have no relation to the actual contribution to the fund. I feel that this action could have been taken long ago, but it is better late than never.
The minister said that while this proposal does not extend to the insured worker who becomes unemployed because of illness, accident or any other reason relating to his health, nevertheless, when the person who has been unemployed for that reason is again available for employment, that fact does not interfere with his obtaining benefits provided suitable work is not available. Of course that situation is not new. That has been the situation right along. If a worker took ill and then upon his recovery reported to the local office but found that suitable employment was not available to him, even if the employment he was now able to take was not the same as that which he had previously taken, nevertheless he then became eligible for benefits, provided he had the necessary contributions to his credit. That therefore is not a new matter.
I am pleased, as I said before, that the minister has brought in this measure. I am sure it will receive the wholehearted support of this committee. Just before I close my remarks-although I know the matter is not pertinent to this measure'-may I say I could have wished that, in considering the regulations governing the act, the minister had seen fit to remove section 5(a)(i). I still have hopes in that direction.

subtopic: PAYMENT TO INSURED PERSONS BECOMING
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we too are glad to see this amendment to the Unemployment Insurance Act. I hope the minister will not mind if I do not congratulate him on bringing it in. I am glad he brought it in. We have been urging such an amendment for years. As he indicated, I doubt whether any large amounts in benefits will be paid out under this provision. Nevertheless, it is a good thing to have the provision in the act so that when a man or woman becomes unemployed, is drawing unemployment insurance benefits, and takes ill during the period of his or her unemployment, he or she, because of that illness, will not be deprived of unemployment insurance benefits.
We have always maintained that when a person is ill and unemployed at the same time, he would surely need assistance more than he did before. I am sorry the minister has not seen fit to bring down an amendment to the act that would make unemployment because of sickness insurable unemployment. The two labour congresses urged this action on the minister in their briefs this year, and I imagine they have done so in other years as well. I believe the fund could well stand that burden at the present time without any

increase in the contributions made by employees, employers or the government. As at the end of December, 1952, the fund stood at over $778 million. I figured out that last year the fund grew by about $9,500,000 a month and that, at the present time, assuming the same rate of growth in the fund has continued, the unemployment insurance fund amounts to well over $800 million.
I do not think the government should ever allow a period of unemployment to develop to such an extent as was provided for when the Unemployment Insurance Act was first passed. I believe it was intended to carry an unemployment load of approximately 10 per cent over a period of time.
I am particularly glad, though, that the minister proposes to make this amendment at the present time. I have found that many persons covered by the Unemployment Insurance Act have felt that merely by contributing to the fund they have been .building up a reserve on which they could draw at any time, even upon retirement from work whatever the reason for retirement. I know that some people who should know better were telling insured persons that that right did exist, that a pool had accumulated in their name in the fund which belonged to them, and on which they were entitled to draw.
I have always realized that this is an insurance measure, and that unless a contributor met the requirement of being involuntarily unemployed, he was no more entitled to draw anything out of the fund than a person contributing to fire insurance could draw from that fund if he had suffered no loss by fire. I have been paying fire insurance premiums on my house since 1913, and shall continue to do so unless I decide to sell the house and live in rented quarters. But I am entitled to no return on the premiums I have paid, other than the protection I am given in case of fire.
Under this measure, which I am sure the house will accept, we will meet a certain physical need, and I believe also a psychological need. I would hope, however, that the unemployment insurance commission might have under consideration the fact that unemployment through illness should be covered by the act. I believe the time has come when that can be done. While we have to accept this as being satisfactory for the moment, I am sure that some day in the not too distant future we shall have the other as well.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to say only a few words at this time. I take this opportunity to congratulate the minister- and I believe I would be correct in using that word-upon having introduced this legislation.
It is a good thing that occasionally we have general elections. I am not suggesting the minister brought this legislation down for

any political purpose; but it does seem to me that just before elections we get things done that we have been trying for years to have done. I am sure all hon. members interested in labour problems will be pleased to see this measure.
A number of us have been pressing for legislation of this kind. I can remember that on many occasions in the house I have pointed out instances in my own riding and in other places where men who had been receiving unemployment insurance became ill, and after that were physically unable to attend at the unemployment insurance office to receive their cheques. Because of that they have been barred from unemployment insurance, through a condition beyond their control. Work has not been available for them, but because of their illness they have been disqualified.
It would appear that the government recognizes that this was an unfair practice, and should be remedied. After all these years, during which we have been pressing for a remedy, it is now brought in. Therefore I believe the minister deserves some credit even at this late date for introducing the legislation. He is the only minister we have had who has seen fit to do it.
I shall not discuss the matter at greater length, because I have done so on many other occasions. This party has always supported a measure of this kind, and we are now glad to see that action is being taken.

Mr. Chairman, I should iike to add a word of congratulation to the minister, and to join in what has been said by hon. members who have immediately preceded me in this discussion. This measure is one the benefits of which will be far-reaching, and I am sure one which will be greatly appreciated in my constituency. Mr. Chairman, as my colleague, the hon. member for Vancouver East, has said, we in this group are glad to see this legislation being brought down. Humphrey Mitchell. On that occasion, and this is the only one I can recall, we were given a little vocal support by a Liberal, the then hon. member for Vancouver North, now the Minister of Fisheries.
That support came about in this way. The hon. member for Vancouver East and I had mentioned cases of individuals who had received unemployment insurance benefits but had been cut off because they had sub-

Unemployment Insurance Act sequently taken ill. Those who remember our late friend, the Hon. Humphrey Mitchell, can well realize the sort of reply he gave us. He said he had never heard of cases of that kind and that if we would just send over our material to him on a confidential basis he would have the matter looked into, but he did not believe it just because somebody had written to us about it. The matters were not confidential, so far as we were concerned at any rate, and both the hon. member for Vancouver East and I indicated that we would give evidence of this type of hardship to the minister. As I say, on that occasion-and it was the only occasion across the years that any support came to us from any Liberal on the floor of the house-the then hon. member for Vancouver North, now the Minister of Fisheries, said, as reported on page 3115 of Hansard:
I can tell the minister it is not an unusual case. I know of several such cases in the shipyards of North Vancouver, where men went on unemployment insurance and then became ill. There was still no work for them, but their benefits were cut off. Whatever minute saving might be made cannot compare as against the distress to such a man who, if he needed the benefits when he was well, certainly needed them far more when he was sick.
So much for the debate of 1948. When we laid the issue squarely before the then minister of labour, we got nowhere with it. I find on looking into Hansard for 1949 that on April 4, as reported on page 2309, we from this group raised this question again. On that occasion we endeavoured, as we had on other occasions, to make crystal-clear what we were asking for. Then I would refer also to page 2882 of Hansard for December 3, 1949. In other words, we raised it in both April and December of that year. As reported on that page, I said:
I propose to deal with just one of the changes that could be made. I shall review it briefly because I have done it on a number of occasions. I am sure I need only to outline my contention to remind the Minister of Labour of the various points in the argument. It has to do with the case of a worker who becomes unemployed, qualifies for unemployment insurance benefits, and then while drawing those benefits becomes ill. As the minister knows, in that situation the worker's 'unemployment insurance benefits are cut off even though there may still be no employment for him.
That is taken from my remarks on December 3, 1949. I might say also there were order paper questions on pages 441 and 1395 of Hansard of the second session of 1949 showing our persistence in our efforts to persuade the government to deal with this matter.
In 1951, when the present minister had assumed the portfolio, we debated the matter on June 30, and the record will be found starting at page 5000 of Hansard. Anyone who

is interested will find that in 1952 we raised this matter on three occasions, on June 4, June 10 and June 18.
By that time we were at least getting the Minister of Labour to admit to us that this was something that was being studied, but that was as far as we could get. As a matter of fact, even when the minister did tell us that the matter was being studied he said also that this involved the whole question of a broad sickness benefit program which was really in the field of health insurance. So we were not given a great deal of encouragement that action would be taken on this matter.
We raised the matter again this year in the form of questions on the order paper on February 4, which can be found on pages 1602 and 1603 of Hansard. I put a number of questions which I shall not take the time to read because they are in this session's Hansard. The upshot of the answers was that the problem was a difficult one and the advisory committee of the unemployment insurance commission were still studying it, but there was no action as yet.
We kept at it and no longer ago than March 25, as hon. members will remember, I asked, this time on the orders of the day, whether legislation of this nature would be brought down at this session. On that occasion the minister expressed his regret that he was not in a position to answer my question. Believe it or not, I felt that was the most hopeful reply we had had in five years. On all previous occasions we were given answers which were clearly in the negative, but when the minister was not able to give an answer I dared to hope that the matter was really under consideration. In view of the fact that an election was not far off-I see tonight's paper says it is to be on August 10 -I hoped that we might get action at this session.
As I say, we welcome this. Of course we welcome it because we have been asking for it persistently across the years, and without a great deal of the kind of support that is being expressed for it today. I think the record should be clear that this is something that is given by this government only under pressure. It is also given because of certain other developments that have taken place recently. The labour congresses, as the minister indicated in the oblique reference he made in his remarks a while ago, are asking for something more than this. They are asking for a program of sickness benefits to be included in the unemployment insurance legislation, which of course is not met by the amendment the minister is now making.
I am sure that as soon as this phase of the matter has been acted upon by the passing of

this amending bill the government will have from the labour congresses a request that the provisions be extended to include anyone who is paying into the fund and is out of work because of illness. As a matter of fact it will not be very long until the minister and his officials will run into that situation. They will find that there will be people who are ill and who are drawing benefits by virtue of the fact that at the time they were laid off they were well, and there will be others who have paid into the fund for some considerable period, who are off work because of illness and who will not be entitled to draw benefits. In some cases workers living side by side will be receiving different treatment. That is a discrepancy which may be explained technically and legally, but it will be most annoying to the workers concerned. The government may as well face the fact that there will be great pressure to extend this principle to include a broad program of sickness benefits.
I have referred to the number of occasions in the past when we have asked for the legislation which is now being introduced. I may say that each time we have asked for it we have suggested that what we were asking for was just a step in the direction of a more complete program, so that now that we are getting this step we express the hope that it will not be long until the government will move on to a wider program of sickness benefits, either as part of the unemployment insurance legislation or as part of a national health insurance program.
I have had occasion previously to read from this little booklet which I hold in my hand, but I think it is appropriate that I should pick it up again on this occasion. This is a very interesting little booklet entitled "Canada Plans Security", by George F. Davidson. Dr. Davidson is now deputy minister of welfare in the Department of National Health and Welfare, but he was not a federal civil servant when he wrote this booklet. It was written in the Canadian forces series, those little booklets that were produced for the troops overseas during world war II so they might be acquainted with what was going on back home. Dr. Davidson, in his very well written little booklet, told the troops overseas what plans were being made back home in the realm of social security. On pages 12 and 13 he says this:
There still remains the problem of loss of Income due to sickness. Unemployment insurance only covers the worker who has lost a job and is still available for employment. If you are sick, you aren't available for employment-so you don't get unemployment insurance.
Unemployment Insurance Act
Then Dr. Davidson went on to say this: Once health insurance is finally put into operation, it probably won't be long until the Unemployment Insurance Act is amended to provide for payment of benefits during the period of a workman's illness. If that happens then a worker off for sickness would get unemployment insurance sickness benefit to make up for lost wages and would have his medical and hospital expenses met out of the health insurance fund-to which he has been contributing.
It would appear that back in 1944 Dr. Davidson was hopeful that the government of Canada would not too long delay the introduction of a health insurance program, and it was his view that as soon as that had taken place, then whoever was the minister of labour would introduce an appropriate amendment to the Unemployment Insurance Act to provide for sickness benefits to be included in that legislation.
It is a shame that we have had to wait so long for national health insurance. I am glad the Minister of Labour has finally decided that he cannot wait any longer for his colleague, the Minister of National Health and Welfare, to bring in that legislation, and has decided that without any further delay at least this step should be taken in relation to unemployment insurance benefits. This is a step toward the fulfilment of one plank in a health insurance program, from which there is no turning back, and just as it was indicated to the men in the forces in 1944 that it would not be long until there would be sickness benefits for workers when they were oil work because of illness, I think that hope should be implemented in a more complete manner than is indicated by the legislation now being introduced. I hope this will be the impetus toward a complete health insurance program.
There is another aspect of this question about which I should like to say a word. One of the reasons I am glad the minister has taken this step is that there has been certain agitation on the part of employers in the country to reduce the amount of the premium. That agitation of course is based on the fact that the fund has grown to a considerable size, and to some people it does seem a plausible step to take. In my view-and this is the view of the labour congresses and the view of the average worker-the step to take is not to reduce the premiums that workers or employers are required to pay, but to increase the benefits paid out of the fund.
After all, a reduction of a cent a day would mean nothing to the average worker, but an increase in the benefit would really mean something to him. I am glad that the minister, faced with the agitation arising from the fact that the fund has become so large, has
4746	HOUSE OF
Unemployment Insurance Act decided that any step he does take should be in the direction of increasing the benefits rather than in the direction of reducing the premium. I remind the minister that on one .previous occasion, I believe it was on June 4, 1952, I had something to say about overfunding of the unemployment insurance fund. In particular I drew to his attention the views of the Canadian Congress of Labour as expressed in the Canadian Unionist of May, 1952. In that issue of that publication Professor John S. Morgan, who is an authority on these matters, was quoted, and the congress expressed its own view that a fund of this sort should not be funded so high that you have this generation paying for the security of the next or a later generation.
As these authorities point out, it is better to put it on something like a ten-year basis so that those who are paying premiums get the benefit of what they are paying, although there should be a certain minimum below which the fund should not fall. But the time comes when the size of the fund really requires either that the premiums be reduced or that the benefits be increased, and I submit that as between those two choices the one to follow is to increase the benefits.
We are glad this measure moves in that direction. We think the minister could have moved further by meeting the desire of the congresses that sickness of workers covered by the unemployment insurance fund be provided for generally. But at any rate we have got our foot in the door on this issue. We are getting something that can be called a form of sickness benefit, but I hope it will not be long until we have sickness benefits for workers generally at the time when they need them, and that they will be related to and integrated into an over-all health insurance program at an early date.
I hope the minister will not mind if we in this corner do not speak on this occasion in quite the congratulatory terms that members of his own party are using. He has been here through the years and has witnessed the fight that we have put up for this step. Therefore we are glad to see it taken, but I hope it will be recognized as what it is, certainly as what it should be, only a step toward wider protection of the workers of the country against the loss of income they suffer not only because of loss of employment but on account of illness.

speechtext: May I ask the minister a question? Would the benefit be payable in the case of an employee who, after he has become unemployed, is injured in his own home?

Oh, yes, Mr. Chairman; it will not matter where the worker may have been


injured. The important point is whether he is unemployed and whether he is already in receipt of unemployment insurance.

subtopic: PAYMENT TO INSURED PERSONS BECOMING
speechtext: Will the employee be penalized if he happens to incur a chronic disease rather than a temporary illness? For example, under the hospital insurance plan of British Columbia a great deal of difficulty has been caused through the attempt to differentiate between an acute illness and a chronic illness. The person with a chronic illness does not get hospital insurance paid while he is laid up. I hope there will be no such distinction in the case of the benefit to be provided by the bill to follow the resolution. In other words, I would hope that any illness will be covered regardless of whether it is temporary or turns out to be a chronic illness.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: PAYMENT TO INSURED PERSONS BECOMING
speechtext: Perhaps I could best explain by stating an example. When a worker becomes unemployed because of lack of employment he has six waiting days, counting the noncompensable day. We will assume that at the end of the six days our office rules that he has 100 benefit days to his credit. If he continued to be unemployed, he would receive benefits for 100 days. Should he become ill, injured or in quarantine during that period, while in receipt of unemployment insurance benefits, he would be able to draw benefits up to the 100 days and no longer.

subtopic: PAYMENT TO INSURED PERSONS BECOMING
speechtext: If it should turn out that he had an incurable disease, he would be able to draw the full amount of the benefits standing to his credit?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: PAYMENT TO INSURED PERSONS BECOMING
speechtext: But not beyond the number of days for which unemployment benefits would otherwise stand to his credit.

subtopic: PAYMENT TO INSURED PERSONS BECOMING
speechtext: What happens if an employee becomes unemployed because he is ill?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: PAYMENT TO INSURED PERSONS BECOMING
speechtext: I am sorry, I did not hear the hon. member.

subtopic: PAYMENT TO INSURED PERSONS BECOMING
speechtext: Does the minister not think there should be some measure on our statute books which would protect that employee?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: PAYMENT TO INSURED PERSONS BECOMING

May I ask the minister whether he means to say that the employee, in the circumstances which he illustrated, would be eligible for his full 100 days' benefits

whether employment was offered to him within that time or not?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: PAYMENT TO INSURED PERSONS BECOMING
speechtext: Well, Mr. Chairman, my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre indicated in his remarks that a long period has passed during which this matter was under discussion, and he was also anxious to keep the record straight. I would like to tell him that in the files I inherited in the unemployment insurance commission there was a report of a study made, starting back in 1949, to which he referred a while ago. I would like to say that out of respect for my predecessor. The question just raised is one of many that have come up in that study in trying to visualize administration. I think I can say that, technically, if there is employment available to that worker in receipt of unemployment insurance while sick, our officials should cut him off.

subtopic: PAYMENT TO INSURED PERSONS BECOMING
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: PAYMENT TO INSURED PERSONS BECOMING
speechtext: But I will say that we do not propose to have doctors and social workers go and find out.

subtopic: PAYMENT TO INSURED PERSONS BECOMING
speechtext: I think that is a very important point, if the department is prepared to go so far as to extend those benefits to the man for the total period that is due to him despite the fact that employment is available subsequent to his illness. I think the house should know whether that is the case. It is going quite a step, and I think when the minister brings down the bill he should make that point clear.

subtopic: PAYMENT TO INSURED PERSONS BECOMING
speechtext:
I would like to add a word to what has been said this afternoon. I do so as a new member who has only been here one session. Irrespective of who argued this resolution and that the act be amended to give these benefits, I think the main thing we should be happy about is that workers in the factories who are dependent upon unemployment insurance benefits will be pleased about this resolution being brought forward by the Minister of Labour. They will benefit from that action.
I wish to commend the Minister of Labour, to congratulate him and also those who have urged in years gone by that this legislation be passed. I hope this is only a first step, and that the government will keep in mind that it is only a first step toward the revamping of the whole Unemployment Insurance Act. I realize that when the legislation was instituted finances were very scarce and naturally benefits had to be held to a minimum. With the large amount of money that has now been accumulated under the act, I feel that further steps should be taken to implement and amend the act so that workers during times of unemployment will receive benefits.
Fair Employment Practices
I have in mind a matter that I shall probably raise when the estimates are before us; and I refer to supplementary benefits. The ben-fits themselves were increased last July, but supplementary benefits were left as they were prior to that time. I think they should be increased in conformity with the benefits.
I wish to congratulate the minister on what he has done, and I am sure it will be welcomed by all people.

Mr. Chairman, I think the amendments which the minister will move in due time and which were suggested by the committee have substantially improved the bill. I must say that I am in complete accord with every one of them, and I think the committee as a whole was in accord with the recommendations which were finally for-

Fair Employment Practices warded. There were some who were opposed, and some representations were made in opposition to the bill, but I think those who did oppose were under a misapprehension. I am sure that in the course of time it will be adequately demonstrated to them that they were under some misapprehension as to the intent of the bill. I am quite sure that none will suffer by reason of this legislation.
There is only one other comment I would like to make, and it is that I still regret that provision was not made in this bill for an educational program. I think the whole matter of education should go hand in hand with the administration of this bill. I know you cannot promote such a program unless provision is made to pay the cost of it. The very fact that no provision is made for an appropriation for this work would indicate that there is no intention to proceed with it. I do not mean to say that there is no intention to proceed with the administration of this act, because I understand that plans are already under way to take care of it within the existing structure of the department. I feel that the officers of the department are fairly well loaded down with work, and that at best it could not receive the attention which is due to such an important piece of legislation. As I said on a previous occasion, I see no provision in the bill for the educational program which I am certain is necessary if this legislation is to attain its full scope.

Ever since this matter was under consideration, without mentioning the verboten word "education" in this house, I have always considered that section 10 on page 5 of the bill takes care of the situation. It reads as follows:
The minister where he deems it expedient may undertake or cause to be undertaken such inquiries and other measures as appear advisable to him to promote the purposes of the act.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PREVENT DISCRIMINATION ON GROUNDS OF RACE, NATIONAL ORIGIN, COLOUR OR RELIGION
speechtext: I hope the minister will follow this up very seriously. I am sure that if he does so he will find that it is necessary to make some provision in his estimates for the necessary expenses.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PREVENT DISCRIMINATION ON GROUNDS OF RACE, NATIONAL ORIGIN, COLOUR OR RELIGION
speechtext:
I can affirm, as the previous speakers have done already, what you said, sir, about the careful study given to this bill by the committee on industrial relations, of which I have the honour to be a member. We heard representations from many bodies. Their briefs were well prepared and useful. We in this group did not agree with the briefs that expressed some opposition to this bill, but at any rate even those briefs were

a contribution in that they provoked discussion in the committee. When the bill was finally passed by the committee, it was a very definite and deliberate decision on the part of the committee on industrial relations.
We are glad to know that the minister, on behalf of the government, is prepared to accept the amendments that were made to the bill in the committee. I believe there were four of them, two of which were not necessary in my view but to which we have no objection. The other two were very important. They were among the changes that were proposed when we debated this bill at the second reading stage, and were recommended to the house by my colleague the hon. member for Winnipeg North. I refer in particular to the change whereby "national origin" is made to include nationality as well as ancestry. I refer also to the change whereby application forms and other methods of inquiry are added to advertisements in the section which outlines certain prohibitions.
