As was indicated earlier by my colleague the member for Winnipeg North, and by others, we too feel that there is a real importance to the educational process as part of this effort to eliminate prejudice as well as discrimination which is the result of prejudice, and I am glad to know that the minister takes seriously the rights in that connection that are given to him under section 10 of the bill.
Because we all agree, and because we are all in support of the bill, it is unnecessary to speak at length. I did feel, however, on the behalf of this party, that I should express our pleasure that the bill has been introduced, and our pleasure that it is being enacted by parliament at this time.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PREVENT DISCRIMINATION ON GROUNDS OF RACE, NATIONAL ORIGIN, COLOUR OR RELIGION
speechtext:
I should like to say a word on this bill, since I was a member of the committee on industrial relations. I do not intend to speak at great length because the committee all agreed that the bill should pass. I was glad to have the minister's explanation of section 10. If you will recall, sir, when this question was first brought up in the house this year, I expressed the view that I did not think you could get the people to accept a measure such as this merely by enacting a piece of legislation or by creating an offence. I said I thought something more had to accompany this measure, and that was education.

The question did come up in the committee, and now the minister has explained that in his judgment section 10 of the bill covers some form of education. I want to join with those who have expressed the belief that one of the essentials necessary to carrying out the hopes expressed in this bill is an extensive educational program. The amendments were agreed to by the committee, Mr. Chairman, and as one of the members of the committee I agreed to the bill, so I do not think it is necessary to say any more at this time.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PREVENT DISCRIMINATION ON GROUNDS OF RACE, NATIONAL ORIGIN, COLOUR OR RELIGION
speechtext:
Before the committee commences a study of the bill section by section, I have a few general remarks to make for which I ask the indulgence of the house. I read carefully, Mr. Chairman, the remarks made by the minister and other members who spoke on this measure when it was presented for second reading. While, like everyone else, I am in complete agreement with the bill, I should like to present for the consideration of the committee some additional observations.
Frequent reference has been made by hon. members who spoke on this measure to the proclamation -by the United Nations Organization on December 10, 1948, of the universal declaration of human rights. The salient feature of this document merits emphasis and re-emphasis. This brief section reads as follows:
All human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights. They are endowed with reason and conscience and should act towards one another in a spirit of brotherhood.
That is the end of the quotation, Mr. Chairman. The doctrine in itself is not new. It is as old as civilization itself. It has been repeatedly enunciated by the ancient prophets, and took its most significant form in the golden rule. We must recognize, however, painful though it may be, that through the ages mankind has unfortunately deviated considerably from its basic teachings. This disregard for the most elementary human law is largely responsible for the greatest tragedies in history. A return to this basic concept is what the world now seeks. This was very eloquently underscored recently by one of our -contemporary philosophers when he stated:
Science has annihilated time and space. A world that has grown geographically smaller, must in the nature of things grow morally and spiritually larger. Brotherhood once a dream and once a vision has now become a necessity-a dire necessity. Unless we develop mentally and spiritually to the same degree that we have developed mechanically and technologically, we shall have, we will have, created a Frankenstein, that will turn around and crush its very maker. Unless we return to first 68108-300i
Fair Employment Practices
and basic principles in human relations the birth certificate of the atomic age may well become the burial certificate of civilization.
It is obviously, Mr. Chairman, not necessary today to argue in a democratic legislative body the legal grounds for the equality of mankind, and although the present legislation is motivated by this moral theory, it should not by the remotest stretch of imagination be interpreted that our country has been unaware of it.
I am satisfied that this bill aims merely to emphasize this principle for those in our country who, in their dealings with some of their fellow Canadians, permit their sense of fairness to become frozen and somewhat distorted by whim, prejudice, intolerance, unawareness or even quite unintentionally, and therefore are inclined to deviate from this basic human law.
I should like at this point, Mr. Chairman, to cite another very pointed statement on. this subject, and I quote from a recent address by J. L. Mann of Chicago. He said:
If prejudice were to be abolished, discrimination would be non-existent; if prejudice were abolished, we would no longer proclaim the fatherhood of God in our houses of worship and destroy the brotherhood of man everywhere else. If prejudice were abolished, man's inhumanity to man would be eliminated; if prejudice were abolished, fair employment practices legislation would not be necessary.
This quotation reflects most admirably the principal objectives of the present bill, and I am therefore happy indeed to join my colleagues in the chamber who almost unanimously support it.
This bill, Mr. Chairman, proudly carries the same stamp of advanced thinking that has characterized all the other social justice measures adopted by this government during the present and the previous parliaments, and will, like the others, evoke the fullest commendation not only from all sides of this house, from the people of Canada, but also from every democratic person everywhere.
Legislation dealing with fair employment -practices is not new to parliaments and other legislative bodies in our country. As has been pointed out, a number of our provincial legislatures and municipal councils have already adopted such laws, and many others are now dealing with similar legislation. But, Mr. Chairman, since labour problems in a general way look for their solution to their immediate surroundings, they necessarily fall within the jurisdiction sometimes of municipal, sometimes of provincial, and sometimes of federal legislative bodies. '
It is comforting, therefore, to find that, in so far as the federal government can possibly reach into and have a word to say

Fair Employment Practices constitutionally about fairness in labour relations, the Minister of Labour and our government, by this bill, express a desire to eliminate unfair discrimination in labour in all those fields of employment which are listed in the bill and which, by law, fall within the jurisdiction of this parliament. For this, Mr. Chairman, the minister and the government merit the gratitude of every employee in Canada.
There are, however, a number of suggestions which I should like the minister to consider in relation to the scope of the present bill in its application. Some of these suggestions may make the measure more effective, because they propose to penetrate a little bit deeper into the field of industry, and reach beyond the limitations set up in this bill.
However, before I deal with these suggestions permit me, Mr. Chairman, in glancing at the background for the consideration of this bill, briefly to draw attention to what contemporary legislative history on the American continent has recorded on this matter.
It appears that immediately following the close of the war in 1945, fair-minded leaders of public opinion were struck by the inhuman havoc which resulted from sheer intolerance and discrimination. Their thinking was directed toward preventing, in so far as it was humanly possible, a repetition of these conditions.
One of the first steps taken was the adoption by the state of New York of the Ives-Quinn law to which the minister referred when he presented the bill for second reading. This law banned social and religious discrimination in employment. It was fathered by the Hon. Irving M. Ives, then a member of the New York state legislature and now a United States senator, and he took great pride in the fact that this law was the first in human history to make the forthright declaration that the opportunity to obtain employment without discrimination because of race, creed, colour or national origin was recognized as a civil right.
From this springboard, Mr. Chairman, there followed in various states of the union a series of bills that gave expression in similar and in more formidable terms to the just human philosophy encompassed in the piece of legislation presented by Mr. Ives. Whilst I have not at hand the accurate number of state legislatures of the United States which have adopted fair employment laws, I am under the impression that a great number of the states of the union now have such measures on their statute books.

Without wishing to burden the committee, but merely for the purpose of indicating some of the considerations which form the basis for the fair employment laws adopted by many legislative bodies, I desire to quote the preamble of the bill of the state of Ohio. I do so because I consider this preamble to be classical and a model followed by most of the states in the union. In some there may be slight modifications in the wording, but the spirit and intent of the legislation is maintained throughout. This is the preamble to the Ohio statute:
This act shall be deemed an exercise of the police power of the state for the protection of the public welfare, prosperity, safety, health and peace of the people of this state and to promote the common good; and the legislature hereby finds and declares that practices of discrimination against any of its inhabitants because of race, religious creed, colour or national origin are a matter of state concern; that such discrimination threatens the rights and privileges of its inhabitants and menaces the institutions and foundation of a free democratic state by fomenting domestic strife and unrest and by depriving large segments of the population of earnings necessary to maintain decent standards of living, thereby necessitating their resort to public relief and intensifying group conflicts.
The right to obtain employment and the right to work without discrimination because of race, colour, religious creed, national origin or ancestry is hereby declared to be a civil right and privilege of the inhabitants of the state.
To move a little bit closer to home, Mr. Chairman, it is stimulating to know that three years before Senator Ives formulated what he calls the first record in human history to enact such legislation, our own government, in 1942, dealt very effectively with the matter of unfair employment practices on the administrative even though not on the legislative level.
On November 7, 1942, during the war, Mr. Elliott Little, who was then the head of the national selective service, promulgated regulation No. 81. This promulgation should be a source of great pride to all Canadians, and in this spirit I desire to read into Hansard a portion of the directive which Mr. Little then issued to regional superintendents and managers serving under the jurisdiction of the Department of Labour. Mr. Little stated:
Some employers continue to discriminate against certain classes of persons on grounds of citizenship, race, language, name, creed or colour. Such discrimination impairs the war effort. No official of selective service should do anything to encourage or facilitate any such discrimination. No such official should make any remark or ask any question of any applicant or employer that could be interpreted as condoning or suggesting discrimination in employment.
Local and regional offices will withdraw from use any employment or selective service forms or questionnaires which contain any question or indication of a person's race, creed, colour, and no form with any such question shall be put into use without head office approval.

If it comes to the attention of a national selective service officer that any employer is unreasonably refusing to engage otherwise qualified persons referred to him by the office principally on the grounds which are discriminatory within the meaning of these instructions, the national selective service officer shall notify such employer that, in view of the evidence of discrimination, he is required to refer the matter to head office, at Ottawa, and that the result may be directions to grant no more permits until such time as it is satisfactorily established that such discrimination has stopped.
No advertisement shall be approved under the provisions of part V of the national selective service regulations if it contains any expression such as "Gentiles preferred", "Protestants only" or any other expression which is indicative of an employer's intention to discriminate against any class of person.
It is of course most gratifying to all of us, Mr. Chairman, that our country can genuinely say that it took effective steps before anyone else thought of doing so, notwithstanding the statement by the Hon. Mr. [ves.
Then followed the Saskatchewan bill of rights act, 1947, which based the law on the human considerations disclosed by its section 8, which reads as follows:
Every person and every class of persons shall enjoy ^the right to obtain and retain employment without discrimination with respect to the compensation, terms, conditions or privileges of employment because of the race, creed, religion, colour or ethnic or national origin of such person or class of persons.
The province of Ontario was next to step in line when on April 5, 1951, it adopted the fair employment practices act. The brief preamble to this act has already been mentioned by the hon. member for Spadina, but it is so all-inclusive that, at the risk of redundancy, I desire to refer to it once more. It says:
Whereas it is contrary to public policy in Ontario to discriminate against men and women in respect of their employment because of race, creed, colour, nationality, ancestry or place of origin; and whereas it is desirable to enact a measure designed to promote observances of this principle: and whereas to do so is in accord with the universal declaration of human rights as proclaimed by the United Nations, therefore His Majesty-
And so on. Then followed the Winnipeg city council, which only very recently adopted a most effective resolution, not only itself supporting fair employment practices legislation but also urging the province of Manitoba and the federal government likewise to adopt similar laws. The province of Manitoba did only a few days ago, on April 30, adopt such a law and I am hopeful that before this day is over this parliament, too, will adopt the bill now before us. There are a number of other Canadian legislative bodies now projecting similar laws. All this is due to the progress of our times and the universal desire to live in peace, harmony and understanding.
Fair Employment Practices
Notwithstanding this, however, I do not think anyone in this house or out of it could justifiably say that discrimination in employment in Canada does not exist, despite our pious hopes and wishes to the contrary. It does exist. We all know it. To say otherwise is a denial of the truth. Countless examples of discrimination are almost common and public knowledge. Everyone is unanimous that it should be eliminated. The approaches to cure this iniquity are manifold.
We all agree that education is without a doubt the most effective method of dealing with it. On this point I quote a brief extract from an editorial which appeared a short while ago in the Chatham Daily News, entitled, "The Root of Discrimination." Amongst the things the editor said was the following:
Prejudice dwells in the human mind, and the only cure for it is to broaden and enlighten the minds of people. This is not a job for the police, but for the churches, the schools and the newspapers.
Of course, Mr. Chairman, the editor could have gone a little further and pointed out that psychologists have determined that no one is bom with prejudices. This is a product of environment and is developed from association with parents, teachers, playmates, newspapers, radio, television, and the like, all of which may serve as instrumentalities of indoctrination.
The editor is no doubt on the right track, but it must also be borne in mind that by the same process of reasoning that no one is born with prejudices, we are told by sociologists that no one is born a thief, a forger, a swindler or murderer; yet there is legislation enacted to attempt to minimize the commission of these offences.
If, therefore, a person with a prejudice confines it to his own personal way of life, and if through his acts others do not suffer, he may stay confined to his thinking and his distorted belief; but the moment his actions interfere with our social structure and tend to deprive others of the liberties, freedoms and rights which this blessed country has given them to enjoy, such a person is guilty of an offence, and should be sanctioned.
Although it is true, Mr. Chairman, that we may not be able to legislate prejudice out of the hearts of people, I am nevertheless convinced that it is possible to legislate the manifestation of that prejudice out of their actions, and thereby minimize the danger of disturbing the peace, order and good government of the community in which they live and work.

Fair Employment Practices
I go along with those who believe that you cannot abolish by legislation the commission of the offences enumerated in the Criminal Code, and that you cannot by law convert a thief into an honest man. But most certainly the Criminal Code intends to protect society against thieves and criminals, and lays down regulations in an attempt to provide the maximum protection possible by the threat of punishment to those who commit the offences.
Consequently it is clear to me, in any event, that the present bill does not intend to legislate against a person's right to his opinions, ideas or even prejudices, but rather to protect society from suffering as a result of his overt acts of discrimination, and from an invasion of its rights and privileges.
I agree with the editor and all those who say that education is perhaps the greatest instrument society has for the elimination of prejudice. But it is also a well-known principle that legislation, accompanied by salutary sanctions, is one of the best educational vehicles in such matters.
I was distressed to read in the press a few days ago that the Canadian Chamber of Commerce has expressed a doubt as to the workability of the proposed legislation. Although the chamber declared its adherence to the principles enunciated in the bill, it seemed to lay emphasis on the fact that education and moral persuasion would prove more effective than legislation, and therefore doubted the need for an act of parliament as an exercise of pressure, which is foreign to the solution of any real problem arising out of discriminatory practices. This is an astounding process of reasoning. No. value whatsoever is placed by the chamber on legislation as one of the processes of education.
I would like to draw to the attention of the gentlemen responsible for the letter which they addressed to the chairman of the parliamentary committee on industrial relations about this matter, a most instructive article which appeared in a publication entitled, "Food for Thought", published by the Canadian association for adult education, and reported in its edition of October, 1949. This is written by Dr. Manfred Saalheimer, and says:
Nobody will deny the importance of education as an ally of legislation. It is certainly not a case of "either-or". It is the case of education plus legislation. Both are valid approaches, complementary to each other. It is also a case of education through legislation. Public discussions on appropriate government control by which evil practices can be ended, parliamentary debate, and finally administrative and judicial enforcement practices will all in themselves be effective educational processes.

And again:
Even the ten commandments had to be reinforced by legal sanctions. If someone objects that killing of human beings continues, despite the sixth commandment and the legal penalties attached to its breach, the answer is that life is certainly better protected with these criminal sanctions than without.
Ninety per cent of our population are fair and law-abiding citizens who are guided by the standards which society has recognized. Thus, if the law indicates that public policy is opposed to hiring procedures based on race, religion, colour or national origin, the bulk of the people will not only conform but will recognize the fair practices as the only right ones. Reference may be in order to the days when bills were introduced in England against child labour. By their public discussion long before their actual passage, an educational process was begun which was continued by their final enactment and by their very enforcement- until the new pattern of conduct was firmly accepted.
I am therefore satisfied that the committee and the house will agree with me that legislation not only proposes education, but supports it; it implements it, it crowns the process of education. That is without a doubt the primary objective of this measure, and that is why it has such wide and almost universal acceptance. The chamber of commerce also expressed some apprehension as to whether legislation of this type can effectively be applied in the general field of industry. On this point I respectfully submit that there could be no doubt about the constitutional position of the bill, because it is based on those matters which fall within the legislative authority of this parliament, and on contractual rights and obligations purely and simply. In the latter case there is created a bilateral agreement by which the government as one party declares that it is prepared to enter into a contract with the second party under definite terms and conditions, some of which are set forth in the legislation before the house. I emphasize that it is purely a voluntary arrangement.
To bulwark the position taken by the government we need but realize that payment for the work performed by those who contract with the government is made out of the consolidated revenues of Canada. These revenues come from moneys received from all people in Canada, irrespective of race, religion, colour or nationality. In other words, every resident of Canada who pays federal taxes of any kind is almost personally a contracting party with those engaged by the government and who are paid out of its consolidated revenues. How illogical it would therefore be for a contractor to take the position that he is willing to accept money irrespective of its race, colour or creed, so to speak, and yet refuse to employ those

very people who in a measure help to provide this money for his remuneration.
A system which supports this view is the one adopted by the United States early this year. A new administrative procedure was designed to effectively implement federal regulations banning discrimination in hiring by private firms working on government contracts. This administrative procedure was included in the general services administration, which is the federal government buying agency, and was announced by Mr. Jesse Larson, head of the agency. Mr. Larson said that his office would be able under the new procedure to persuade a contractor to either meet the requirements of the regulations banning discrimination, or to cancel his contract: This new recommendation was suggested in a report of the president's committee on government contract compliance which was presented to President Truman immediately before his term expired. The adoption of our bill will make it possible for the Canadian government to follow a similar procedure in our country, and it is my conviction that it should be done.
I said earlier in my remarks that there are a number of suggestions that I would like the minister to consider. It is my humble belief that the bill could go further in its application. I would like to see much more direct provision to indicate that the effect of this act will make it possible to penetrate industry in whatever form it takes as a result of the contractual arrangements with the government. There are thousands of employees working on government general construction, public buildings and public works; many more thousands working on defence projects, the manufacture of uniforms, equipment, supplies, etc., all of which are produced under contract between the government and independent industrial and commercial bodies.
In studying this measure now section by section I hope hon. members will consider the importance of making the act apply to all employees who handle the whole or any portion of these operations, payment for which is made out of the consolidated revenues of Canada. This act should extend to every phase of employment over which the government has control either directly or indirectly.
On this point I draw attention to the fact that no mention is made in the bill about the responsibilities of a subcontractor. I urge that categoric provision should be made that the obligations undertaken by the contractor should apply also in every detail to all and
Fair Employment Practices any of his subcontractors. This will prevent an escape by the contractor who may plead that a breach was committed by a subcontractor and not by himself. In having the bill extend to subcontractors, an additional safeguard is provided against the abuses which the law seeks to prevent.
In the same spirit, I would like to see the bill extend not only to independent contractors or subcontractors in the general sense but to anyone who is under contract with the government for any purpose whatsoever, and one of the tests to determine this contractual position should be whether or not moneys are used which come from the consolidated revenues of Canada. This would also bring into focus any loan corporation, insurance company, or other financial institution which makes loans out of moneys supplied in whole or in part by the government of Canada, when such moneys are to be used for building or other projects undertaken upon the recommendation or with the approval of the government of Canada, irrespective of whether such moneys are provided by the government in the form of loans, grants, subsidies or guarantees.
The Minister of Labour in his remarks drew to the attention of the house the fact that at the commencement of this year directions were issued by order in council that all contracts with the government must include a non-discriminatory clause with respect to labour used by the contractor concerned. This is indeed an effective beginning to implement the spirit of non-discriminatory legislation, and the present bill will continue to blaze the trail in this field of social justice by giving it the necessary force of legislative authority.
I would like now, Mr. Chairman, to say a word about another type of discrimination in labour. The hon. member for Hamilton West has presented Bill No. 188 dealing with the question of providing equal pay for equal work for women. The underlying intent of Bill No. 188 is the desire to deal with this additional form of discrimination-

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, it is my intention to avail myself of this opportunity to deal with a subject that has been discussed at different times in the house on earlier occasions, and for that very reason it is not necessary to enlarge upon the details. Nevertheless there are certain points with regard to the subject which I should like to bring again to the attention of members of the house, and to seek from the house a statement as to the policy which is to be adopted by the parliament of Canada and by the government from time to time which represents it.

What is the subject?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
We have talked so frequently about our resources that we have come to discuss them without recognizing how revolutionary events of the past few years have been. We always knew we had immense resources. We knew that in some cases we had more than any other country in the world. Now we find ourselves suddenly confronted with the fact that here in Canada are known to exist the most important resources upon which the industrial strength of any nation can be built.
We knew that we had the greatest commercial forests in the world, we knew that we produced most of the world's nickel, we knew that we produced more than half of the world's asbestos, we knew that with imported bauxite we were one of the -greatest producers of aluminum, we knew that we had an immense reserve of coal, we knew we had iron, we knew we had oil and natural gas, but it is only within these last few years that we have suddenly come to realize that we have the greatest known resources of iron ore in the world today, that we have the greatest known reserves of coal, that we have the greatest reserves of oil if we include the tar sands of Alberta with our known resources, and -that above all we have in this modern atomic age that remarkable mineral, uranium.
We might have iron and other raw materials and still not be one of the greatest industrial producers. That depends upon power and human skill. We have the human skill. We demonstrated that during the great war by the things of the finest type that we have produced in this country. Also these are the things which are needed for industrial production-coal, water power, oil, natural gas, and now uranium. We have all five. Without too much knowledge of what Russia may possess today, we know that of the countries which disclose their possessions we are the only important country that has all five of the sources of power upon which industrial production is built.
We have a fantastic inventory of minerals. We are therefore confronted with a decision, and an urgent decision, as to what our policies will be. Canada was confronted with a similar decision some 40 years ago when the exhaustion of the forest resources of the United States imposed demands upon our forest resources which might easily have dissipated them in the same way. A decision of vital importance was made at that time. It was decided that Canada was going to use its forest resources for the legitimate selfinterests of Canada. As a result of that decision the value of our forest products has

multiplied more than ten times since 1910, and today the greatest dollar earner in Canada for the people and workers of Canada is the forest industry of our country.
Today we are confronted with the necessity for a similar decision in relation to our mineral and other irreplaceable resources. Upon that decision will depend the kind of country Canada will be in the years ahead. I submit that there is no more important decision facing the people of Canada, represented here in parliament, than a decision as to the policy that is to be adopted in this respect. If in application to these resources which are more difficult to conserve, and which cannot be replaced in the way that forest resources can, we adopt a policy similar to that adopted 40 years ago with respect to our forest resources, we will not merely increase our wealth but we shall emerge within a comparatively few years as one of the great powers of the world. Within 25 years we may have a population of 30 million, within 50 years a population of from 60 to 100 million. The size of Canada, the future of Canada, depend upon the decision that we make. We are still awaiting a declaration of policy in these critical days.
We must remember that the provincial governments have the primary authority; nevertheless this is a field for close cooperation. Today the government of Canada is called upon time and time again to enter into contracts related to the use of resources, to take various steps related to this use, and what is done will depend upon the policy that is adopted. If we make the right decision today this will be the dawn of the development of a new world power, Canada, such as we have scarcely dreamed of up to this time.
If I may, Mr. Speaker, I should like to read the amendment I have in mind. It will only take a minute, and if I have the indulgence of the house I shall do so and conclude my remarks because I have already put my views with respect to the subject on record in much more detail on earlier occasions. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker):
That all the words after "that" to the end of the question be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
whereas the natural resources of Canada are a heritage that should be developed and conserved for the purpose of providing the greatest possible measure of opportunity and security for all Canadians, this house is of the opinion that immediate consideration should be given to a national policy under a system of free enterprise and in close association and collaboration with the provinces that will:

(b)	protect and conserve our forest, mineral and other resources from undue depletion or exhaustion;
(c)	expand the use of our resources for industrial production in Canada and thus create greater opportunities for the employment, advancement and security of all Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, exactly the same amendment, word for word, was moved by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) on June 16, 1952, and it can be found in Hansard of that date at page 3263. I intend to move exactly the same subamendment as my leader moved on the same day, and it can be found in Hansard at page 3267.
I am going to be very brief in speaking to this amendment to the amendment, but I speak for a few minutes because the C.C.F. is fundamentally and primarily interested in the conservation of human and natural resources. It is the basis of our national policy and of our approach to political, economic and social conditions. This has been demonstrated repeatedly by speeches made in this house throughout the years, by members representing this group, and in successive national and provincial conventions of the C.C.F. All those conventions took considerable time in discussing the very problem we have before us this evening.
Last session, and again this session, I moved the following resolution:
That in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of calling a dominion-provincial conference on conservation with a view to the establishment of a national policy on soil, forest and water conservation and land use for Canada.
I did that on behalf of this group because we believed that this problem must be kept before the house, and was one in which a large number of people in this country were concerned. We find from correspondence we have, as do other members of the house, from organizations all across this country and from

Natural Resources
individuals, that the problem is receiving increasing recognition. When the resolution on this subject was being discussed this session, its importance was recognized by the interesting debate we had, in which members of all parties took part.
Now, Mr. Speaker, when we come to deal with natural resources as a whole we are covering a very wide field. We are covering our water resources, our power resources, our forest resources, our mineral resources, and our soil resources, and the question of erosion as it affects our streams, lakes and river shore lines in this country. We agree largely with the resolution moved by the Leader of the Opposition, but we do not agree with two or three words which indicate that he wants to restrict the development of our natural resources entirely to free enterprise.
I understand that because it is strictly in accord with the Progressive Conservative party's economic theories. In doing so, however, I think they show a certain amount of inconsistency, because we have the large publicly-owned hydro development in Ontario, and the public power developments in Saskatchewan and British Columbia as well as in the other provinces. Why do we have these? Because free enterprise, in which the hon. gentleman believes, refuses to accept its responsibilities in that respect. The people could not receive from free enterprise the service they are receiving today from the publicly-owned development of the natural resources for power purposes.
Even this government has recognized that it is necessary for the government to undertake the protection of our natural resources. It is for that reason the government undertakes conservation measures through P.F.R.A. It has done excellent work. Why have they undertaken that work in the prairie provinces, to some extent in British Columbia and in the marshlands of the maritime provinces? This government has undertaken that work because it recognizes that free enterprise will not accept any responsibility, and recognizes too that the work can only be undertaken satisfactorily under government direction and government auspices.
Mr. Speaker, I think there is some inconsistency in the point of view of the Leader of the Opposition because in recent days we have had a very lengthy debate on the Saskatchewan dam. Is the hon. gentleman suggesting that free enterprise build the Saskatchewan dam and conserve the natural resources of Saskatchewan in that respect? No; he and his colleagues wholeheartedly support the public development of the Saskatchewan dam to protect and conserve the natural resources of that province.

In addition to that, the public development of natural resources is receiving ever wider recognition. Look at the federal government's policy in respect to the conservation of forest resources, limited as it is. Who accepts the responsibility for co-operating with the provinces in the development of better fire protection, the development of insect control and fungus disease control? Who conducts the investigation? Who gets the evidence? Who takes action? The federal and provincial governments do that co-operatively. Why? Because free enterprise will not accept its responsibility toward the preservation of our natural forest resources.
Then we come to the question of erosion. Who protects our shores? Who is asked to develop an erosion policy for Ontario lakes and the lakes in British Columbia? The federal and provincial governments recognize that free enterprise will not accept any responsibility with respect to that.
I intend to be brief, because we do not want to hold up the house at this time. We in this group believe wholeheartedly in a national policy of development in co-operation with the provinces for the conservation of all our natural resources. We believe it is very necessary that such a policy should be inaugurated as soon as possible. We propose that the best way to develop and preserve and protect our natural resources is by a combination of public co-operative and private ownership. As is evidenced from our wasting soil in the maritimes, our wasting timber in Ontario, our abandoned farms in Ontario and even British Columbia, the loss in fertility of the soils in recent years, we believe that free enterprise, in a wide section of the development and protection of our natural resources, has completely failed during the years to recognize its responsibility, and in some instances is not as capable of undertaking that protection and development as a government, federal or provincial.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I take pleasure in moving a subamendment, seconded by the member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis), as follows:
That the amendment be amended by deleting therefrom the words "under a system of free enterprise and"
The resolution would then read as follows:
That all the words after "that" to the end of the question be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
"Whereas the natural resources of Canada are a heritage that should be developed and conserved for the purpose of providing the greatest possible measure of opportunity and security for all Canadians, this house is of the opinion that immediate consideration should be given to a national policy in close association and collaboration with the provinces that will:
(a)	promote and develop all the country's natural resources for the benefit of the people of every part of Canada;

(b)	protect and conserve our forest, mineral and
other resources from	undue depletion or
exhaustion;
(c)	expand the use of our resources for industrial production in Canada and thus create greater opportunities for the employment, advancement and security of all Canadians".

Mr. Speaker, I think no one in the house had expected that the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) would move this amendment this afternoon, at this late date. For the life of me I cannot quite understand why he moved it at this time unless, of course, he sincerely feels that this is a topic of such great importance that it must be debated in the house every few weeks or months. As my friend the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) has said, it is not long since the Leader of the Opposition moved exactly the same resolution; and at that time I think it was debated at length in the house. Whether we like it or not just at the moment, the resolution has been moved and I suppose it is up to us to state our position on it. I therefore propose to do that in just a few minutes tonight.
Let me make it plain, Mr. Speaker, that I am all for having topics of such great importance as this one given every possible consideration by the members of this house. If there is one subject that is of more importance than another to the people of Canada, I think it is that of the proper development, conservation and use of our natural resources. In anything I say tonight I must not indicate that I feel that is not an extremely important consideration for every Canadian.
One could speak at great length on the terms of the resolution. Every single one of them is full of meat and involves such important considerations that, in the period of 40 minutes which is alloted to each of us, it would be impossible to begin to deal with the things that should be dealt with. However, Mr. Speaker, I should like just to say a few words in a general fashion to indicate how we feel about the resolution and also, in the course of what I have to say, to indicate how we feel about the C.C.F. subamendment.
The subamendment just moved by the hon. member for Kootenay West would delete from the amendment the words "under a system of free enterprise and". Mr. Speaker, I am not afraid of the term "free enterprise"; not at all. Of course, when we are speaking of free enterprise I think we ought to be prepared to define our terms. I think we should be prepared to state specifically what we think free enterprise means; and I believe I am prepared to do that.
Natural Resources
So far as we are concerned, Mr. Speaker, we believe that in our economy proper recognition should be given to private enterprise. We believe that private enterprise ought to be preserved most carefully. I think one of the outstanding contributions which our province has made to the strength of Canada as a whole has been its demonstration that private enterprise, relieved of some of the burdens that are generally placed upon it and shorn of some of the abuses which sometimes attend it, can serve humanity well and can work successfully to produce goods and services in abundance. Private enterprise can yield enough and to spare for all human beings. I am satisfied of that fact. Believing that, we feel that every opportunity should be given for the fullest measure of the exercise of private enterprise in the development of our resources.
But there is this important point that we must keep in our minds. In my province we have had quite a good deal of experience now with the development of resources and the laying down of policies for doing so. Using an interesting combination of private-enterprise activity and wise and efficient government policy, I think the province of Alberta has not only shown the rest of Canada that the natural resources of a country can be developed in an orderly fashion, but has gone beyond that and also demonstrated that this combination of wise government policy -and private-enterprise activity can develop resources in such a way as to make them yield to the people substantial revenues which can be used to replace taxation or to supplement it in providing the people with services.
I recall with considerable and, I believe, pardonable satisfaction how during the early years of my first experience in government we laid down policies which we felt convinced would induce an orderly development of our resources in the province for the good of all our people. We kept in mind at that time the need for preserving the private-enterprise principle because, under that principle, we were certain that human beings would make their best efforts and produce the best results. We introduced a system of leases, rentals and royalties covering all of our resources. We provided inducement, wherever possible, for exploration and development; and as a consequence of the assurance that they would be given a good run for their money, individuals and groups of individuals brought capital into the province and invested it as risk capital to develop the resources.
Those people who brought their money in and invested it were given a run for their

Natural Resources
money, and in not one single instance did we break faith with them. As a consequence we obtained orderly development, and development in the best interests of the people; and it will stand comparison or contrast with the development that can be demonstrated in any other province in Canada. Having said that, I hope I have made clear just where we stand with respect to this matter of private enterprise. We want to preserve that principle and at the same time we want to see that our resources are developed.
The resolution moved by the Leader of the Opposition goes beyond that and sets out three specific clauses to indicate the kind of natural resources development and protection the Conservative party would stand for. The first clause reads in this way:
-in close association and collaboration with the provinces that will:
(a) promote and develop all the country's natural resources for the benefit of the people of every part of Canada:
In his extremely short speech the Leader of the Opposition this afternoon indicated that he understood that the natural resources belonged to the provinces and that the development of those resources would have to be primarily the responsibility of the provincial governments. But he did say the federal government ought to work in very close collaboration with the provinces and lay down a national policy of co-operation and assistance to see that the resources were developed for the benefit of the people of every part of Canada.
I notice that in paragraphs (a), (b) and (c) there is an indication of something the Leader of the Opposition said a while ago in the course of another debate. He seems to indicate throughout the whole of his amendment his desire to see a Canada first policy introduced into this country. I may' say that during the course of the pipe-line debate in the house not long ago I heard him say that he believed in a Canada first policy. I also heard the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) declare that the Liberal party is a Canada first party.
Well, I should like to tell both these recent converts to Canada first that we Social Credi-ters have been putting forward a real Canada first policy in and out of parliament for the last 15 years. Away back in 1938 the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) moved in the house a resolution in specific terms that put forward a realistic situation and a real Canada first policy that called not only for the development of our resources in the interests of all Canada, but also stating in effect, though perhaps not in these exact words, that whatever policy we do lay down, 
for the development of our resources and the realization of a strong and virile and happy Canada, we must reconcile our national aspirations with economic truth. And he has been saying that-and so have we all-ever since that time.
I have not yet heard the Leader of the Opposition set out in specific terms the kind of national policy for the development of our resources that he seems to feel the government ought to be adopting. I should like to hear the government or the official opposition put forward their views, and I should like to examine them in detail. If we do examine them in detail I guarantee we will not find one single instance in which recognition is given to the necessity for reconciling our national aspirations with economic truth. I would like to see that done, and when it is done I am going to be the first person in the house to congratulate those who put it forward.
There is no sense sitting back and talking about the development of our resources in an orderly fashion for the people of Canada, and at the same time refusing to lay down financial and economic policies that will make it possible for our people to enjoy the fruits of their labours. I think it is about time we began to tie these things together, and to look at them in a realistic fashion.
Time and again we have put forward our proposals in which we do very closely tie in the financial policies with the economic policies for the development of resources. I think that is a realistic Canada first policy.
I should like to bring up for one moment a case in point. Not long ago we discussed here the question of building a pipe line for the transportation of gas across Canada to serve the markets in the east. That was very definitely one of the facets of a national policy. But in the course of the discussion of that pipe-line bill, and the discussion of getting Alberta's gas, which is of tremendous importance to this country, into the markets of eastern Canada, I heard some rather remarkable observations. For instance, I heard the Leader of the Opposition make the statement that he believed the pipe line should follow an all-Canadian route. I heard the Minister of Trade and Commerce stand in his place and declare that it must follow an allCanadian route. I heard him propose this idea, that no licence would be granted for the carrying of gas through a pipe line from the western provinces to eastern Canada by way of United States territory, and that any pipe line carrying that gas must come by an all-Canadian route.
I am not discussing pipe lines, but I am just using this to illustrate what I wish to say. By stating that the pipe line must

follow an all-Canadian route I say that both the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Leader of the Opposition were failing to recognize economic truth. I am not going to say that such a pipe line would not be feasible. Let me hasten to assure the proponents of an all-Canadian pipe line that I hope when all the facts and figures are brought to light an all-Canadian pipe line will be able to justify itself, in the light of economic facts. I do hope so, because I would like to see it all-Canadian for numerous reasons.
But, Mr. Speaker, I am certainly not going to throw this thing into confusion by declaring that it must be so, before I see all the facts. And let me say that no one who has spoken in the house on such a subject has had the facts in front of him to justify an allCanadian route. I would like the Leader of the Opposition

I invite him to do so-to supply me with facts upon which he would base the statement that an all-Canadian pipe line to carry Alberta gas from the west to the eastern markets is feasible, and not only is feasible but will carry the gas to the east and lay it down in the eastern markets at a price which will yield a reasonable return to the people producing the gas at well-head. The well-head price is important.
I would ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce to produce for me the figures and facts, and until he does so I must conclude that he cannot. Further than that I am going to say it is dangerous and foolish for any of us to rise in the House of Commons and take a firm position in a matter of that kind before we know the facts. All I want is the facts. When I get them I will be able to make up my mind which is going to be the most feasible and economic route, and one which will yield a reasonable return to our country. I am concerned about all sections of our country. I am concerned about producers; I am concerned about consumers. In the development of all our resources I would like to see a policy adopted that would ensure both reasonable protection, and a reasonable promise of return for what they do and what they buy.
This Canada first policy applies not only to gas but to the development of all our resources. In adopting a Canada first policy I think it ought to be definitely understood that if the kind of Canada first policy proposed by the Liberals or the Progressive Conservatives is going to cost any particular section of the Canadian people any amount of money, either the producers or the consumers, then I say the government ought to be prepared to make that up by means of
Natural Resources
subsidies. That is the position we take. That is realistic.
To come back to the illustration of the pipe line, which can serve as an illustration for all of our national policies in the field of resources and development, if the selection of an all-Canada route for the transportation of gas eastward is going to cost the producers more money, if it is going to depress their price in the west, then the government that adopts that policy ought to be prepared to step in and subsidize those producers so they will not lose money.
So it should be with the consumers. If by following an all-Canada route to get gas east into the market the price is pushed up, whereas if you had followed some other route you could keep the consumer price down, then I say it is up to the government that introduces such a policy to see to it that the consumers are subsidized so that they do not have to pay for the sentiment that the government would weave into a policy.
We believe in Canada first; we believe that sentiment should play its part. But we submit that that part ought to be cut to the bare minimum. We should look at facts and see to it that our policies reflect the facts and are in consonance always with economic truth. That is the policy we follow. We would like to see a national policy laid down. I do not believe there has been any such policy; in the field of fuel there certainly has not been.
We have been following a hit-and-miss, patchwork policy all during the years. I am not blaming just this government, as it seems to have become a habit. I think it is about time this government sat down with the governments of the provinces and worked out a national policy that will cut sentiment to its bare minimum but keep sentiment there, sentiment in favour of Canada. I am satisfied that they would have no trouble whatever in getting support.
I think that is about all I want to say at this time, but I do want to indicate that we are indeed Canada firsters who would attempt to reconcile national aspirations with the truths of economics.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member should explain to the house how these idealistic "Sacred" policies are now working out in the province of British Columbia, where they have managed to close a great number of saw mills and many mines. I have not seen any indication yet of the government of British Columbia coming along with any bonus or compensation for the people who have been put out of business as the result of those "Socred" policies.

Natural Resources
Better look to their predecessors and find out what they did to put them out of business.

Mr. Speaker, this amendment is one of the most important to have been introduced in this house, as it deals with one of the most important matters we could possibly deal with at the moment; but it has received treatment at the hands of the C.C.F. and Social Credit parties which needs some explanation.
From what the C.C.F. have said there seems to be a misunderstanding as to the meanings of conservation and development. They are two entirely different things. The fact that it was a Conservative, Sir Adam Beck, who developed the policy of municipal ownership, development and distribution of hydroelectric power is quite different from saying that it should be a government's job to go and look for mineral deposits or for oil wells. The distribution and development of hydroelectric power is one thing. It is the conservation of the flow of a river, a national asset, and the development of that asset for the greatest good of the greatest number. That has been the policy of Ontario governments, I think, since 1911. It has been found to be economically sound and it has now been adopted by and large by nearly all the other provinces of Canada. That is one thing.
You have rivers such as the Niagara and the St. Lawrence, great national assets belonging to the Canadian people. Nobody found them, or I suppose it can be said that originally the Indians found Niagara and the St. Lawrence. Nobody discovered water power, or at least it was generally discovered that water and gravity would produce electricity. Electricity is a great national asset and its distribution for the greatest good has been a fixed policy in the country for the last 40 years. But it has fallen down in some places. There have been places where the policy has failed, and there are signs that it is not living up to its promise in some localities.
But the development and distribution of electricity is an entirely different thing from the search for and development of an ore body. I happen to be a small shareholder in an oil company. This company has drilled 18 dry wells. What sort of explanation would I as a member of the government give to this house if I had to say that we had drilled 18 dry wells, had spent so many million dollars, and had nothing to show for it? What would the position be? Is it the function of government to engage in the speculative

development of natural resources? That is obviously not the case.
Only one out of 156 mining developments ever comes into profitable production. It used to be one out of 100, but now it is one out of 156. If I were spending the public money could I come before this house and say, "Mr. Speaker, I am sorry that only one out of every 156 times I have spent the people's money has paid off". What sort of reception would I get? What sort of reception would any government in this country get if they went into that sort of business.
Let us lay this nonsense about governments going into mining once and for all. Take the case of uranium. Uranium was developed and became known as a metal vitally needed for the atomic bomb. It was nationalized by edict of the government, at a time of war; and the Eldorado Mining and Refining Limited-it was a gold mining company at one time-was taken over by the government because it had this essential resource necessary for the development of the atomic bomb. At that time the atomic bomb was thought to be the one weapon with which we could bring about peace.
What has happened? The government took over all prospecting. The government took over and completely clamped down on anybody looking for uranium. The government created a monopoly in uranium. But Mr. Speaker, that monopoly failed; and if it had not been for private enterprise, the small prospector, developing such areas as Beaver-lodge and all the other areas, uranium development in Canada would have stopped where it was in 1945 and 1946 and we would not have any more uranium. Instead of being about the first uranium producing country in the world, we would have been simply a third-rate power in the production of uranium. It has been private enterprise, private money, risk capital that has developed uranium. Without that risk capital uranium production today would have been confined to one or two deposits which were known before.
Who are the people who today go out with the geiger counters? Who are the people who go out today looking for this radioactive material? They are the individual prospectors, the small companies if you like, the large companies if you like, but private enterprise. The government has failed, as any government would fail and must fail, to develop a great natural resource like uranium.
I now come to the question of pipe lines. I would not have mentioned pipe lines had it not been brought up by the leader of the Social Credit party (Mr. Low). Natural gas is like electricity. It is a natural asset of

this country. It can be compared with electricity as a fuel of development. There are two problems to be solved. The first problem is simply this. There is a tremendous surplus of natural gas in Alberta at the present time, and a market for that gas must be found as soon as we can possibly find it. That is problem number one. Problem number two is this. If we ship that natural gas to the immediate market in the United States, can we work out a quid pro quo with the United States so that the gas-hungry east of Canada will receive cubic foot for cubic foot?
Mr. Speaker, in all history no arrangement with the United States has ever been worked out on that basis, and with the intractable attitude of the United States government and the United States congress it is extremely unlikely that any government of Canada could possibly work out an agreement such as that with the United States. In view of our complete inability to work out a treaty like the general agreement on tariffs and trade, under which they will not even accept our dairy produce and in view of the fact that they are now introducing tariffs against lead and zinc-there are already 43 bills excluding Canadian produce at some stage or other in the United States congress at the present time-what sort of chance would we have to work out a quid pro quo in natural gas with people who take that view of international agreements, Mr. Speaker? We would be fooling ourselves.
Here we have a great section of northern Canada, the northern part of Ontario, rich in minerals, rich in nickel, rich in copper, rich in all the precious and base metals which the country and the world must have, but deficient in fuel. Are we going to ship our fuel to another country and allow that north country to remain a barren waste, with the ore under the ground and never developed? Or are we going to try in every way we can to develop that country through our Canadian fuel which we have in such abundance? Surely it is worth while, even though it costs us in Toronto a little more for our natural gas to see that north country developed. There are nickel deposits at Emo; there are the new developments at Sudbury which are worth having developed by our own natural gas.
That is what I mean by a Canada first policy. Let us look after our own developments. Let us bridge the boundaries that run north and south. Let us look at the boundaries that are put there by geology. Let us forget for a time the political boundaries and develop this country on the geological boundaries. If we do that we shall not only be creating new wealth, but we shall be populating that barren territory which is the bugbear
Natural Resources
of all our transportation problems. We shall be putting people and mines and developments in there; we shall be building other Sudburys, several of them, in that great northern territory which today lies barren and must lie barren unless fuel is brought to it. That is what we mean by a Canada first policy. Let us see that that country is properly developed.
I want to make a protest against this government and this house. For 25 years the committee on mines, forests and waters has been set up, and never once has it met. Never once has this parliament of Canada, certainly in my time, considered it worth while to go into the development of our natural resources. We set up the committee. It was a sinecure. We allowed the dust bowls to develop in the Palliser triangle; we allowed our rivers to erode; we allowed our mines to be high-graded; we allowed our natural resources to go to waste. Never once did this parliament take the trouble to look into the development and the conservation of our natural resources. We are a people, Mr. Speaker, whose parliament is so negligent in its basic duty to preserve the very life, the soil, the water, the minerals which make us what we are as Canadians. These could make this the happiest, the most prized land in all the world, yet here in this parliament we do nothing about it. Do we deserve to be the happy land we are? And how much time have we before we find ourselves a have-not country, before we have the situation indicated by the devastating evidence brought down in the Paley report in the United States.
There is my criticism, Mr. Speaker, of what we have done. Our sins have been sins of omission. We have thought we were living in a perpetual boom, a perpetual holiday, and what has happened? The truth is only now coming home to roost; and it is not coming as roosters, it is coming with the carrion claws of socialism; it is coming on the vulture wings of get-rich political schemes. That is what is happening.
Unless something is done about this, Mr. Speaker, we will find ourselves a have-not country. Time is short. We are losing our raw materials, which are being developed by other people. We are losing our top soil because we have not the wit to see that the development is such that the very life of this country is being blown away and we are doing virtually nothing about it. If during my presence in this house I did nothing more than make this protest against our policy, I would still feel myself justified. The time is short, Mr. Speaker. The laughter of two members of my own party who know little and care even less show that this danger is not understood.

That's telling them.	Mr. Hansell: Don't forget the collection.

worried.
