The matter of the development of our natural resources is not something about which we can laugh and jest. One day instead of this being a boom land, Canada will become a have-not country.

Mr. Speaker, as I seconded this subamendment I feel that it is my duty to say a few words on it, though I know that at this stage of the session everyone is interested in getting the debates over as quickly as possible.
This debate, of course, could be termed the big debate. It actually started in June of last year. This motion was put forward by the Leader of the Opposition in exactly the same words, and we proposed an amendment in exactly the same words. Pretty much the same speeches were made, but that will not apply to the one I am going to make now.
The leader of the Social Credit party this evening would lead one to believe that he was opposed to both the amendment and the motion; but I would like to remind him, in ease he has forgotten and wants to be consistent, that members of his party voted for the amendment which we proposed last June. This debate came on rather quickly, and they may not have had a chance to look at the record.
We do not need to look to know the record.

I really enjoyed the speech of the hon. member for York West (Mr. Adamson). He was the complete demonstration of the story about the lawyer who says, "When your case is weak, holler as loud as you can". He made a very loud speech tonight, so I said to myself that the hon. member for York West was on shaky ground and was trying to accomplish his purpose by making a loud noise and letting us believe that he had a lot of ammunition. But his speech was very good.
Thank you very much.

I am going to try to stay as close to the point as possible and in order to do so I will follow the practice of the average clergyman. He must preach a sermon on a particular subject on Sunday, so he takes a look at the Good Book and finds a quotation. He takes that quotation as his premise, and builds his case around it. That is what I am going to do now.

The hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bryce) can look after that. The amendment of the Leader of the Opposition suggests that he is very much concerned about the development of Canada's resources for Canadians. That is a very good principle to advocate at any time but in his motion he is not giving all Canadians an opportunity to participate in the development of those resources. He limits his motion to the development of our resources by free enterprise.
What is free enterprise? Well, generally in this country it is a group of people who have enough money go out to develop resources which they think will be most profitable to them.
They hire a man with a pick and shovel.

Well, the fellow with the pick and shovel will do the producing, but the point I am making is that the Leader of the Opposition is restricting the development to some privileged group in the country. The subamendment which we propose merely strikes out the two words "free enterprise", and we accept the rest of the motion. That enables free enterprise to do what they desire or what they can. Our policy is that any group of citizens, regardless of the amount of money they control, should be permitted to do something if they can. On the other hand, if it is not possible to get things done by risk capital or by small groups of individuals we say that it is the responsibility of the government to step in where necessary and develop our basic resources.
In the first analysis the government holds the resources of the country in trust for the people-for all of the people, not just a small group that has some money. I am going to take a quotation from page 3036 of Hansard for 1932. As I said, the clergyman seeks higher authority, quotes that authority and builds his case around it. In this case I am going to quote the late Lord Bennett who was speaking on the very point I am now making, the responsibility of the government as custodian of the natural resources of the country.
He said:
I believe that there is no government in Canada that does not regret today that it has parted with some of these natural resources for considerations wholly inadequate and on terms that do not reflect the principle under which the crown holds the natural resources in trust for all the people.
That is a long way from the motion now proposed by the Leader of the Opposition. You know, the private corporations and com-, panies that have now become popularly known under the term "free enterprise" have

had that chance for many years. At eight o'clock this evening, before coming downstairs, I was listening to the radio. I heard a group of newspapermen and one lady from our press gallery interviewing the premier of Newfoundland, the Hon. Joseph Smallwood. This island operated under that system of free enterprise for a good many years, and at least twice during my lifetime has gone into bankruptcy. A commission of government from Great Britain had to take over the administration of its affairs. Newfoundland is now part of Canada, but all during the time its development was unrestricted by government there was not very much development.
I only heard a little of what Mr. Smallwood had to say, but he pointed out that his government did undertake the responsibility and developed three small industries, which they operated for a time. Later on they sold them, but they drove in the wedge to get industry in that part of the country. It was the initiative, drive and courage of the Newfoundland government that actually got something done. Nothing had been done under the system of free enterprise. Whether or not we agree with what the gentleman did, in my estimation he has done more for that part of the country since he formed the government than was done by all the free enterprisers without government interference.
Are they all paying?

I am not going to argue that point. If you asked me whether or not Canada Packers were paying I would not be able to tell you because they always keep two sets of books, one for public consumption and one for the back office. I am not, therefore, going to start analysing the finances of the government of Newfoundland. However, that is just an example. I am not speaking personally when I say that, because we believe in getting things done for the Canadian people, regardless of who is doing it. If something is being done, we are quite prepared to give credit where credit is due.
As I said a moment ago this slogan that Canada should develop Canadian resources for Canadians is particularly good at election time. However, one should stop for a moment and think of the resources that are left. As the Leader of the Opposition mentioned, our iron ore resources have been farmed out for at least the next ten years. Our oil resources are being piped over to the United States. In this house we moved a motion that the main pipe lines at least should be made common carriers, and that the government should control the main lines and allow
Natural Resources
development to the east, west, north and south from those main lines.
I recall that the leader of the Social Credit party mentioned our fuel development, and that reminded me of another badly managed industry, the coal industry. This industry has been in the hands of private enterprise for a good many years, and today the provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Alberta and British Columbia are smokeless smoke stacks, monuments to the faulty development of that industry. Our coal industry is folding up under the system of private enterprise. We only produce 17 million tons of coal per year in this country, yet we import around 27 million tons. I am convinced that if this industry is to get proper development to the point where it will at least remove Canada's dependence upon the United States for coal, the government is going to have to step in rather than leave it for further exploitation. This was clearly demonstrated during the last war.
However, that is a long story. This industry has been badly managed, and it has been in private hands for a good many years.
I believe that, in the light of these facts, the Leader of the Opposition should agree to eliminate those words "free enterprise". As I pointed out a moment ago these words restrict the development of our resources to a very small group, whereas the amendment to the amendment which we propose opens the thing up. It permits the government to step in where they think it is necessary, and there are many times when it is necessary. We do not want to forget the example of synthetic rubber. When we were badly in need of rubber, and when the secret formula was in the hands of certain people in the United States-I do not want to put the name on record again because it has been done before-the allies did not get the secret formula. It went over to Germany, in accordance with an agreement made previous to the outbreak of war. It is to the credit of this government that, under the direction of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), they established for the first time on this continent a synthetic rubber plant which successfully filled the gap that was created by the loss of our source of rubber in the east.
Risk capital could not be found to develop that industry; it had to be done by the government. Consider housing as another example. There is nothing to stop free enterprise from building houses. There is no rent control any more, and there has not been for years. The house building industry wants all the profits of a gamble and all the security and protection of government guarantees and subsidies. There is nothing to stop them from building houses. The construction industry

Natural Resources
is free. The lumber industry is free. They have hesitated because they want guarantees against losses; they want certain guarantees in so far as profits are concerned. If it were not for what the government is doing with respect to housing and underwriting the risks that are being taken, there would be very little done toward building houses in this country today.
With all due respect to him, this is another indication that the Leader of the Opposition is being unrealistic. He insists upon writing in words that would afford to one section of society only the right to develop our natural resources.
I do not want to continue any longer on this subject, Mr. Speaker. It is one upon which any of us could talk for an hour. It was debated at length last June, and the arguments today are not very different. In order that the house leader may get along to the next order of business I am prepared to rest my case on the statement made by the late Lord Bennett, to the effect that the government are the custodians of the natural resources of the country, and that they hold them in trust for all the people and not just a small group of people. The Leader of the Opposition's motion restricts the development of our resources to one privileged and private group, whereas the amendment we propose opens up the way so that all Canadians, under government direction if necessary and under co-operative development, can share in the future development of the resources of this country.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is, of course, an extremely important subject. It is one that was seriously and, I think, usefully debated in June of 1952. It is raised by this motion which contains some general principles on which I think everybody in this house is agreed and which constitute, if I may use a colloquial term, a sort of bandwagon on which everybody wants to climb; but because of the way in which these general principles, which are acceptable to everybody, are put forward, there will no doubt be differences in the way hon. members of the house are going to vote upon the amendment and the subamendment.
The members of the C.C.F. party say they are quite prepared to accept the form in which the amendment is drafted provided the words "under a system of free enterprise" are struck out. I think the hon. gentlemen who have spoken for the C.C.F. party have gone beyond what is really expressed in the amendment. As I read it, it is not restricted to development by free enterprise. It is merely an assertion that we have in this [Mr. Gillis.i
country a system of free enterprise and also a constitutional system under which the resources are the property of the crown in the right of the provinces, and that therefore the development should take place under a system of free enterprise and in collaboration with the provincial governments.
All that, I think, is something about which all of us agree. I think all of us recognize the fact that there are some things which it is more appropriate to have done by public authorities than by free enterprise. But I think we are all most happy when free enterprise does what is required to be done and public authorities do not have to intervene.
I think that statement is also acceptable to the members of the Social Credit party. They are not wedded to having everything done by free enterprise; like others, they recognize the fact that when free enterprise is doing what is required in a satisfactory way, it involves less responsibility on government bodies and is a more desirable manner of achieving the objectives sought. But what we on this side of the house cannot accept are the statements and implications in the motion that the government is opposed to the application of those principles.
We recognize, as do all other hon. members, that the natural resources of Canada are a heritage to be developed and conserved for the purpose of providing the greatest possible measure of opportunity and security for all Canadians. We recognize that proper government policies are those which promote and develop all the country's natural resources for the benefit of the people of every part of Canada. But of course the owners have special rights that have to be considered in the development of those natural resources for the economy of the whole country. We are ten provinces that are useful to each other. The development of each contributes to the economy of the whole nation, and the economy of the whole nation contributes to the prosperous condition of each of the ten provinces. The amendment states that the policies adopted should be policies designed to protect and conserve our forest, mineral and other resources from undue depletion or exhaustion; and also that they should be policies that would expand the use of our resources for industrial production in Canada and thus create greater opportunities for the employment, advancement and security of all Canadians. I am sure that the Leader of the Opposition and his colleagues recognize, as do the members of the Social Credit party, that all this has to take into account the realities of the conditions and the circumstances.

It is not more than a few days ago since the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) was concerned about the terms of a licence for the exportation of natural gas because the terms under the existing regulations might deter the United States federal power commission from granting a licence for the importation of some of the natural gas into the western United States. That concern was not because the hon. gentleman is not sincerely and genuinely devoted to the principle of Canada first and Canada all the time; it is because the circumstances are such that the natural gas which exists in such great abundance in the Peace river district and in the adjoining district of British Columbia cannot be piped down to Vancouver just for the consumption that can be made in Vancouver and in our Canadian Pacific coast market. In order to find a market for that gas, and to bring it to the assistance of proper development on the Pacific coast it is necessary to invest so much capital that it requires carrying a larger quantity than Vancouver and the Canadian coast can consume. That larger quantity can only find a market in the adjoining western states.
I think most hon. members in the house are satisfied with the policy expressed by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) the other day, and that this situation in British Columbia was because of exceptional conditions; that we could not-as the hon. member for York West (Mr. Adamson) said a moment ago-expect to make a deal whereby, if we supplied so many billion cubic feet of natural gas to one part of the United States, from one part of Canada, we would get back from the United States an equal quantity of their natural gas in another part of Canada. The Minister of Trade and Commerce expressed the view-I am no expert and have not his experience-that it was probable that it would be an economic possibility to complete a pipe line that would pipe natural gas through Canada and find within Canada a sufficient market to justify the expenditure required for that kind of pipe line.
I said we cannot admit the implications and statements that this is contrary to government policy. Hon. members of the house -and I think the legislation went through with the unanimous approval of the whole house-adopted in 1949 the act respecting forest conservation, to authorize the government to collaborate with provincial governments and enter into contractual arrangements with provincial governments for the better conservation and management of the forest resources of the Canadian people. It
Natural Resources
was only this session, I think, that the house again unanimously agreed that it was good policy that was being expressed in Bill No. 109, to authorize the granting of assistance to all provinces for the conservation of water resources. Those two were government measures. I am not taking any special credit for their having been government measures. They are Canadian measures. They are measures desired by Canadians generally for the welfare of Canadians generally.
I think the same kind of applause that has just greeted this statement was heard when the Minister of Resources and Development (Mr. Winters) explained the position of the government with respect to the suggestion- if it was only a suggestion, or application if it amounted to an application-that the water of the uninhabited northwest regions of Canada be diverted into Alaska to develop electricity in that part of United States territory. I think everyone applauded the declaration of the minister that that would not be done at least until it had been ascertained that those resources could not be used to advantage within Canada as motive power for industries to be established in Canada itself.
Then the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) quoted something from the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett, when he was prime minister of Canada. Well, that is something with respect to which one could find other contrasting statements. But it is, nevertheless, the guiding principle that I am sure would be followed by whomsoever had the responsibility of presiding over a government in Canada. There may be diverging views as to the extent to which circumstances require or justify its being applied in one set of circumstances, and the extent to which it could be applied in another set of circumstances. But that is always a matter of judgment. I am convinced that whatever party one professes to belong to, one is anxious in a given set of circumstances to do that which will be best not only for a small group of Canadians, but for Canadians generally, for the development of this country.
We are all equally proud of our Canadian citizenship. We are all equally proud of the vast extent of our country and the great natural resources with which it has been endowed. No doubt we are all believers that the fourteen million-up to nearly fifteen million-people who are Canadians today do not represent the numbers who will be Canadians in half a century or a century from now. And we are all most anxious that those more numerous Canadians have as good reason as we have to be proud of their Canadian citi-

Natural Resources
zenship; and that requires us to be very careful in our management of those natural resources.
I am going to repeat something I have said before; that I was very, very favourably impressed while flying over, during the course of five or six days last September, the western coast of British Columbia and Vancouver island, to see the immense forest resources that we have on that western slope of the Rocky mountains. And I was impressed to see the rapidity with which the terrible damage that, I am told, was caused less than a quarter of a century ago around Trail, had disappeared as a result of the work of nature in reproducing the vegetation of that region.
And taking the poison out of the smoke.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
They took the poison out of the smoke, of course. When they ceased giving off those obnoxious fumes, nature got to work and repaired the damage that had been caused previously, and did it very rapidly and very effectively. As I have already said in the house, just before that I had been up in the lake St. John district and had been impressed by the fact that there was from $125 million to $150 million worth of metal being marketed from that region, to which there was being contributed from the resources of Canada nothing but Canadian labour and the electricity produced by the running streams of our Canadian rivers.
We have made mistakes; but I do not see the picture in as grim a light as was portrayed tonight by the hon. member for York West (Mr. Adamson). Yes, we have made mistakes. But time is not so short; and I think that with honest and sincere co-operation among all levels of government it is still possible to foresee a future where there will be perhaps several times as many Canadians to share the wealth of this country as there are at the present time. We trust they will not feel that we have impaired and permanently damaged the great heritage we received from our forefathers, and that we are going to hand down to them.
It will require things like the Canada Forestry Act; and, more than the act, it will require action under that act. It will require things like an act to authorize the granting of assistance to provinces for the conservation of water resources; and it will require action thereunder.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: What about the South Saskatchewan dam?

The South Saskatchewan dam is a dam that is projected on a river which carries immense quantities of water to

Hudson bay, where it produces no apparent benefit for any Canadian. But the cost of that dam should not have to be of the magnitude pictured in the royal commission's report; or, if it is, I do not think any government would attempt to justify to the Canadian public that it was a prudent investment.
That is something about which there is disagreement, the cost estimated for that project. There are very wide divergencies between the estimates which have been made; and that is something which should be further considered, because no one sitting in the seat before which I stand at the moment would recommend to parliament a thing which he did not believe was a proper investment in the interests not only of a certain portion of the people of Saskatchewan, or even all the people of Saskatchewan, but in the interests of the Canadian economy as a whole.
That is worthy of further consideration, whether or not there be elections in the offing. When elections are in the offing we have to give consideration to the effect of our conduct and the effect of our words upon those who, after all, are our judges. But I believe, and I think most hon. members believe, that the best case we can put before them is that which will induce them to believe that we are being frank and honest with them, and are prepared to take the consequences for the mistakes we make, always being careful to make as few mistakes as possible.
We have to oppose this amendment, not because the general principles are things with which any of us disagree but because we cannot agree that the conduct of the government has been such that we have to be blamed for not properly implementing policies based on those general principles. Instead of the language it does use, had it read-
Whereas the natural resources of Canada are a heritage that should continue to be developed and conserved for the purpose of providing the greatest possible measure of opportunity and security for all Canadians, this house is of the opinion that consideration should continue to be given to a policy which does under a free system and in close association and collaboration with the provinces:
(a)	promote and develop all the country's natural resources;
(b)	protect and conserve our forest, mineral and other resources;
(c)	expand the use of our resources for industrial production in Canada-and thus create greater opportunities for the employment, advancement and security of all Canadians.
-we would, of course, be prepared to agree with it. But hon. gentlemen opposite do not feel they can say that we have been doing that. They must say we have failed to do that, and ask the house to condemn us for having failed to do it. That, of course, is a position we cannot accept. I hope that

there are enough members in the house who feel that we do not deserve condemnation to defeat both the subamendment and the amendment, and I hope there will be in the country enough who will feel that we do not deserve that condemnation to accept the fact that we have voted against this amendment.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I interpret the words of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) the whole issue between us is a difference of words which amounts only to this: We say that immediate consideration should be given to a national policy under a free enterprise system, while the government would have been willing to accept the statement that we continue to give consideration to such a policy. *
I must admit that if the whole division of voting in this house is to rest upon such a refinement of words, then it will seem to be extremely difficult to conceive of a type of resolution that could be framed which would meet the government's sensibilities in matters of this kind.
Perhaps if we collaborated in drawing them up there would not be that difference.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Oh, yes; the government would like to have one party in this house so there would be no division of opinion at all. But we do not believe in a one-party system. We believe in the exchange of ideas under a two-party system, and we do not believe that we must conform to the views of the government in order to be useful members of this parliament.
We have put forward a resolution which, according to the Prime Minister, varies in no way from his ideas except that instead of saying that we wish a continuance of policies of this kind, we say there should be the introduction immediately of a national overall policy of the nature we have described. That, according to the words of the Prime Minister, is the whole issue between us.

I presume the hon. gentleman accepts the qualifications I indicated in my remarks, that we are not to take these terms as being absolutely rigid, that there are circumstances which require some departure from the application of the general principles.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I had intended to come to that, because in that part I agree with what the Prime Minister has said. In so far as his comments related to the views put forward by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) I do agree with him, but when the words "free enterprise" are used as describing the system that we desire, under no reasonable circumstances could it be suggested that we
Natural Resources
are seeking to impose a rigid limitation, that only under a system of free enterprise can any development take place. I must say that it would be peculiarly inconsistent for me to assert that in view of the fact that it has not been so long since I was justifying a rather important undertaking under a publicly-owned system in the province from which I come.
No, I agree that there are cases where, because of the monopolistic character of the production, it is desirable that the government take under its own direction the development of something that is for the general use of all the people and which is not something that can be dealt with under the ordinary competitive terms of a free enterprise system.
Having said that may I go further and say that I do think the hon. member for Cape Breton South has misconceived both the words of the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett, as he was at that time, and the application of the words which he has quoted. He referred to a statement by the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett to the effect that the government is the trustee on behalf of the people of the natural resources of the country. He referred to a statement by the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett that there had been cases where those assets had been disposed of on terms that did not represent their real value at the time they were handed over. That has nothing whatever to do with the belief anyone may hold that there are advantages in a free competitive system. Surely no one is going to suggest here that the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett was an opponent of the competitive system of free men and women upon which the strength of free nations has been built.
I go further and say that we should examine at this time just what is indicated in the suggestion that resources should be placed entirely under the control and operation of the government for their future development. I hope no one will suggest that I am making invidious comparisons when I point out that we can easily see examples of complete ownership and operation. We have it in Russia. We had it in Germany and in other countries.
One of the reasons the free nations of the western world demonstrated greater strength in the war for freedom which took place only a few years ago was the collective strength of free people, where individuals exercised their own intelligence and competed with each other, and produced the results of competition. Those nations were stronger than the nations where the initiative of individuals was submerged under the monolithic state. Our secret weapon in the last world war, the weapon which was most effective in defeating German military might, was the strength of the nations

Natural Resources
where the collective power of free individuals gave to those nations that flexibility that comes only when there is a full belief in the free spirit of men and women.
Freedom is indivisible. We believe in freedom. When we say "free enterprise" we are not for one moment suggesting that the resources of this country be handed over for exploitation by any limited group. That is not what free enterprise means, in spite of what may be said. Certainly there have been abuses under free enterprise, and certainly there have been the most terrible abuses under complete government monopoly of all the powers of the state. As between the two I leave any thoughtful person to judge as to which he would prefer.
There are abuses, and let us make sure that in every way we can, by the collective judgment of free men and women, we eliminate those abuses. But under a proper system of supervision of our resources let us be sure that in this young nation we do not stifle the spirit of our people by handing over to the state the power to place in the hands of men and women whom they appoint the complete responsibility for the development of those resources. Oh, I only wish that everyone could see what happens when that is carried to its extreme. I and others in this house have seen what happened in Russia where the full power of the state is exercised in every segment of human activities. Do not think for one moment that inequalities are ended there. In no country in the world are inequalities greater than in Russia, where it is only the servants of the state who have the luxury, the comfort of position, the automobiles and all the things that go with the prerequisites of office.
No one who has seen state operation carried to its extreme will ever suggest for one moment that, whatever abuses may have occurred here from time to time, they are better under an absolute state monopoly. What we want above all else is to retain the freedom to correct abuses and, under a system which eliminates abuses, invite the competition of free men and women to give to all young Canadians the hope of success in the years ahead by hard work, with the education and spirit that has been given to them.
In so far as the words "free enterprise" are concerned, we certainly placed them in this motion with a definite purpose in view. We want our resources treated as assets that are in fact the assets of all the people of Canada.
I have had occasion before to deal with this situation, and not to speak about it alone; and I have acted in accordance with my own belief that they are assets that belong to all the people of Canada, and that they should

not be made the special privilege of any small group. Nevertheless, when it comes to the actual industry that grows up from the use of those resources, let us retain the advantage of that kind of competition which brings to its full development the spirit of a free people.
Having said that in regard to this motion, and recognizing the sincerity of the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) in putting forward the arguments he has placed on the record in this house, may I say that we agree with him that most certainly there should be no improper exploitation of our resources, and most certainly one section of society should never have a limited advantage which can be conferred upon them. There have been abuses, and doubtless he had some of those abuses in mind when he put his argument forward; but let us all join in insisting upon that type of regulation which will avoid any unfair advantage to any particular group of people but will open to the widest the opportunities that can be made available to our young people, by the hope that can be offered to them that by initiative and hard work they can go out and build their own future as their parents did before them.
In all these things of course there are certain qualifications that must always enter into this subject. I notice it has been said here that we have put forward a view that is not consistent with the best interests of one part of Canada, and perhaps of Canada as a whole, when we have urged that in using the natural gas of this country we should insist upon a policy which gives first consideration to Canadian development. I certainly do not in any way withdraw from the position I have taken that in the use of our natural resources, whether it be natural gas, oil or anything else, we should give first consideration to the development of our own country, and that we should bear in mind that in the use of these resources we have a choice between creating employment for Canadians or employment for others. I have not suggested at any time that we should deny to others the opportunity to use our resources on any basis that does not imperil the continuing availability of those resources for our own development in the years that lie ahead.
I did say, and I repeat now, that in the carrying of natural gas to eastern Canada it is to the advantage not only of eastern Canada but of Alberta itself that the general interests of Canada be considered, and I am convinced that the people of Alberta will be best served if they have the sure and certain markets of Canada available to them rather

than markets which at any time might be interfered with, if they are carrying that gas over a long distance to points where the legal supervision, of the pipe lines will not be under Canadian control. We have put forward our own clear idea of how exchanges of gas and other natural resources can be carried out. But when it comes to the carrying of gas to eastern Canada, we suggest that a Canadian route is preferable to a route which denies to Canadians the ultimate control over the supplies that will be carried in that way.
So far as the main motion is concerned, I regret that the government feels it necessary to draw a fine distinction about the wording. I suggest to the Prime Minister that while in 1949 we had an act respecting forest conservation, and this year we had an act respecting the conservation of water resources, these fall far short of an over-all national policy consistent with the words set out in this motion, which would at this time decide that in future the development for the advantage of Canadians is going to be the first concern in the use of the extraordinarily rich resources that we possess.
A decision of a similar kind was made some time ago in regard to the forest resources to which the Prime Minister has referred. At the time that decision was made members of the Liberal party, as well as members of the Conservative party, joined in a national policy in regard to the use of those resources. We are simply seeking at this time, when fabulous resources have become available to us, to establish a similar policy in regard to these new resources now available; and it is our hope as well that this motion, which does not condemn the government in any terms it contains, but seeks for a declaration of policy, might receive the favourable consideration of hon. members.

Like the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) I wonder what the purpose of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) is in bringing a motion of this kind before the house without giving the rest of us any notice that it is to be made. Just before he sat down he said that this was not a motion condemning the government. But if what he is asking to be done has already been done, why the motion? If it has not been done, then certainly it is a motion condemning the government. As far as I am concerned, that is neither here nor there. The government has many more able people than I to defend their position, and I think the Prime Minister did it very well a moment ago.
Natural Resources
What I want to draw attention to, and what I really rose to speak about, are the amazing series of arguments that the Leader of the Opposition used. He brought Russia into the picture with the idea of giving the impression that those of us who advocate something other than capitalism want the Russian system. The term "free enterprise" is used instead of capitalism. Capitalism got too smelly and they had to get a new name, free enterprise; but, for those of us who do not swallow that hook, line and sinker, he tried to show that we advocate complete control of everything under a dictatorship such as exists in Russia.
The hon. gentleman knows better than that, that we do not want anything of the kind and we would oppose it just as much as he would or those who sit behind him would. But some of us have read history, and we cannot forget what free enterprise or capitalism was when it was really free, before there was any control by government, before there was any enactment of factory laws, before there was any development of the trade unions to protect the workers in industry, before there was any of those things. We know what free enterprise was and we know what capitalism was; and we know what capitalism would be today if it were freed of the controls which socially-minded governments everywhere have imposed upon it.
May I say that all of the great fighting in world war II was not done by the peoples of the free nations. On many occasions I have had to argue against people who would tell me that, because of Russia's fine record in the war, her people having accomplished that great record of achievements, there must surely be something in their system of government that enabled them to do that. In order to show that a good military record was not essentially a matter of good government, all one had to do was point out what the nazi armies had done before the free world and a big section of the totalitarian world got together to stop them.
Tonight the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) tried to explain what he meant by the phrase "under a system of free enterprise". Unfortunately for him the hon. gentleman spoke on that subject when this group moved a similar amendment to a similar motion made by him on June 16, 1952. I read from page 3287 of Hansard for that day. After criticizing some of the statements made by the leader of this group, who at that time, spoke and moved a subamendment, the Leader of the Opposition said:
On the other hand I do not think the record of governments in supervising-

Natural Resources
Note the word "supervising".
-the use of these resources in itself is a very good argument in favour of giving still greater authority to a government not only to supervise but to go apparently a step further and engage in processing as well.
I would like all members of the house to pay particular attention to the next few words.
It was for that very reason that this motion sought to make it clear in advocating the further processing, as well as the conservation of these resources-
Not only the things we have done under various acts of parliament to which the Prime Minister referred but the processing and the conservation of those resources as well.
. . . we believe it is under the free enterprise system that this work will best be carried on and the highest measure of employment will be created.
There you have his real ideas. Not only must processing be carried on without interference by government, but conservation must be carried on without interference by government.
We just do not go along with that at all, because we know what business has done to our natural resources. We also know what conditions in this country were when free enterprise had a free hand, when we had the great depression of the thirties. Let us not forget that it is war and the fear of war that has enabled free enterprise or capitalism to do what we see today. If the prop of war production was pulled out from under it there is nothing to indicate that we would not be back again where we were in the hungry thirties. Instead of there being opportunities for young people there would be nothing better than doss houses and rides on the t6p of freight cars.
I was paired with the hon. member for Chicoutimi (Mr. Gagnon). Had I voted, I would have voted against the amendment to the amendment.
I was paired with the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Wylie). Had I voted, I would have voted against the amendment to the amendment.
